XXIII, is, no doubt, as much disregarded by our contemporary Pharisees as it was by the ancient ones; for unworthy persons, when in power, always pretend to their right, and therefore, though acting ever as treacherously to that very Public, from whom their salary is raked, think themselves justified in doing so, and elevated over censure, þÿ just as, in reality, they are elevated over such reverses of fortune, by which, in private life, a man is rewarded or ruined through the natural results of his own efficiency. Whilst einaiie.ipalloli had, in vjtioe ol die pracucal suite ol matieis and facts, of which die want ol labour and die very resiricied iiuinner of laliouiets ounhi io lie pointed out as particularly important, effected a real identity and conihinalioii ol ihe inteieats of the planters and Inhouiers. it resulted from the sudden n tid levolutionnry lotm under which u look place, thai these interests were speedily regulated with exclusive n defence to what is piaciieiilh necessaty andean be realised here, waving ail auemc's at get- 1 1 1 g tip meie llicottes ot ol nans) larding Monti European social an ) legal itisinuilons. li was c.ettatnlv premised ami umlerstood, Hint the Provisional Ai't niter havini; stood the probe ol a year's lime, would be subjected

to a revision; this has however, in consequence of lamentable events, over which the inhabitants of these islands had 110 control and which at the same lime retarded the reforms, intended and promised to beundertaken in many matters of an administrative nature, not been done; anexperienceof fouryears, which moreover were fruitlul of great difficulties, has now shown that, at any rate in regard to the rural population, the right track has been followed. That it, after the expiration of so lengthened a period and when so many relations, which before were uncertain and unsettled, have consolidated themselves, and it must be added, when at all events a partial progress and development is manifested, the practical effects of which would henceforth appear yet more forcibly under the supposition of some ensuing good years, should be advisable again to make the whole matter the subject of legislation, we can by no means consider raised beyond doubt and absolutely granted. The emanation of a new law on this matter would involve a new regulation of all the relations between planters and labourers, as also a repeated confirmation of what is to be kept and to remain, and therewith a new difficulty for effecting any alterations; eventually it will itself adopt such alterations. The subject itself, the general position and interests of an entire agricultural population, is perhaps according to its nature itself less than any other a hi subject for legislation, as long as not such practical inconveniencies and

deficiencies arc proved to prevail, which can only be remedied by the interference of the State; here, where the estates have already suffeted so much, that the consequences of an erroneous or somehow mistaken measure could perhaps never be effaced, and where the labouring class is by no means disposed and prepared for any kind of new laws, there is double reason for particular and circumspect reserve in this respect. That precisely they are not mature for or require any new laws, is distinctly shown by the very contents of the law-draft and the debates which have taken place. We can thus not acknowledge that under such circumstances any weight ought to be uitached to mere formal considerations. The existing regulations, which for about four tears have been the law of the country, will also in future remain in legal force, as long as the King does not abolish .them, their validity is not dependent of a formal sanction to be given within a certain time or certain years ; up to the moment that they are done away with, their legal force remains the same as that which any new ordinance might be invested with. Relations which affect an entire community and in particular the class in the same that live by the work of their hands, must to a certain extent be, and can at any time be made the object of agitation, but such agitation is certainly more likely to be called forth by a new law, be its contents new or not, than when such an outward occasion is not given. In regard to the real qualities of the mat-

ter, the Provisional Act may contain some purely temporary rules and norms, besides others that are indistinct or erroneous, but these have either been amended or rendered superfluous by practice as also by subsequent ordinances ; these do not afford any sufficient motive for new legislation. Other matters, f. i., the position of estates with regatd to the provision of the poor, we could wish to see regulated by a new law; however existing circumstances, particularly the want of the necessary funds, preclude an efficient measure on this question. In respect to the substance of the now existing regulations, comprising also the principle of annual contracts and the uniform payment for the usual kinds of work, Government has, and certainly with full reason, inserted them in the new draft and thereby corroborated, that they under the given circumstances have proved on the whole well adapted to and in harmony with the real interests of the community and particularly with those of the labourers. As the opinion has often been set forth, particularly by people who are unconnecied with these matters, that the tendency and object of ifiese regulations should be to place the country labourers in u, comparatively speaking, un-

Another view which at the time was propounded by others, and certainly was not meant to be illiberal, that the emancipated labourersshould be regarded and treated as "seivants" was rejected on account of, that such a conception, whilst it in general would degrade them, must hurt their feelings and impede the development of family life. that any difference in cash payment within Ihe same island could not be effected, had become the general standard) was converted into a legal rate of wages, so that the right of the labourers to receive them was secured, that is to say, it was rendered independent of any new arrangement between the planters The right of the grown up labourer to be furnished with a house on the estate, which the latter has to keep in repairs, combined with the certain revenue derived from his labour enables him to tnariy at any time he chooses, free ftom material cares or the dread of having to apply to any poor fund I i is entire position implies that he is sought and valued where he is ; that he knows that his removal would not be liked by any means, and that he would be welcome on anv other estate, that any doubtful mailer would be settled in his favour; he is moreover sure that he will receive his due when no body else receives it, and even that he will receive more. The Dumfries Standard says : þÿ Having observed that one of the titles of the new Empress of France was " Kirkpatrick de Closeburn," our curiosity was excited to know whether she was in any way related to the ancient family the Kirkpatricks of Closeburn, in this neighbourhood. Well, we have had the honour of conversing with a venerable and worthy maiden lady, residing at Nitlibank here þÿ a member of the family of the Kirkpatricks of Conheath, Caerlaverock, a branch of the Kirkpatricks of hagen, with this Island's Produce, | Closebnrn. She informs us that her brother, William Kirkpatrick, became American consul at Malaga Spain, and married into an ancient family of the name of Graves or Gravi, our informant is not certain which. The fruit of this marriage was the mother of the new empress, who married the Count de Montijo. Our venerable friend is theregrand-aunt of the empress herself. " Mak fore aunt of the empress's mother, and Siccar" is the motto of the Kirkpatricks. The empress seems determined to ex- emplify it. We trust she will " mak siccar," for she has a cunning fox to deal with. However, we think better of the emperor than ever, in having the sagacity to marry a Lady of a good old Nitlisdale stock. The following " Affectionate and Christian Address of many Thousands of the Women of the United States of America to their Sisters, the Women of England," is published in the semi- " A common origin, a common faith, and, wc sincerely believe, a common cause, urge us at the present moment to address you on the subject of enormous social evils which still prevail so extensively, and, even under kindly disposed rulers, with such frightful results, in every part of your country. " We approach you to-day, not with fiction, but with fact þÿ not fact as exaggerated, perverted, and discoloured by the novelist's imagination, but fact as presented in its native simplicity by parliamentary documents, or other statistical writings, which are regarded in your land as of standard authority. It will be impossible for us to bring now to your consideration the immense aggregate of evils which are visited upon the poor and helpless by your husbands and brothers through the vast extent of your Sovereign's dominions. We must forbear to speak of the flagitious and bloody modes by which those dominions have been extended and are now extending in Southern Africa, in Southern Asia, and through the Southern Seas ! We can say nothing of the iniquitous war your nation waged upon the Chinese, or of the untold miseries caused by the forced imposition of the opium traffic upon that people ; not even for poor Ireland can we invoke your sympathies now þÿ that land which, through British misrule, has decreas-

ed in population 20 per cent, within the last year, and of which one of your own admired writers þÿ the Rev. Sydney Smith þÿ wrote these words, as awful as they are true 'So great and so long þÿ has been the misgovernment of that country, that we verily believe the empire would be much stronger if everything were open sea between England and the Atlantic, and if skates and codfish swam over the fair land of Ulster.' Sisters, we suppress our indiguation, and touch upon none of those things now. It is upon evils on your own soil, in your own communities þÿ evils among which you daily live and move, and with which you have personally to do, that we now address you. We wish to speak to you of the ignorant, and the poverty-stricken, and the degraded population of your own land, and we shall do it with faithfulness, yet with kindness. " Sisters, your land is filled with slaves þÿ slaves to ignorance, slaves to penury, and slaves to vice. The terrible truth has been told you by one of the most learned and respected authors, Joseph Kay Trinity College, Cambridge, at the close of of his great work on national education, which is, or ought to be, familiar to you land, ' where the aristocracy is richer and more all, that in Engpowerful than that of any other country in the i delity with which we have to deal. If we do not world, the poor are more oppressed, more pauperised, more numerous in comparison to the other classes, more irreligious, and very much worse educated than the poor of any other Euro-

pean nation, solely excepting uncivilised Russia and Turkey, enslaved Italy, misgoverned Portugal, and revolutionised Spain.' The first and greatest of all popular needs in every free Christian country is the need of instruction and ; yet your country has no system of public education that is worthy of the name. The entire amount of your annual Parliamentary appropriations for the education of your people is less by thousands of pounds than the annual public expenditures made for this purpose by the city of New York alone. One person out of every eight in your population is a pauper, and the average poor rates of England for the last, ten years have been £6,000,000 ; and yet to provide public educa-

v & © n St tion, and thus in a great measure remedy the very neglect which has cursed you with this grievous and yearly increasing burden, your national Legislature has expended in six years only £600,000. One-third of the population of the State of New York, according to our census tables just published, are regularly receiving education in our public schools ; according to our parliamentary returns, only one-eleventh of your population are weekly Courier and New York Enquirer : þÿ enjoying a similar advantage. Sisters, is that a Christian state of society which, for some millions of your people, renders the development and cultivation of all those faculties which distinguish man from the brute little better than a physical impossibility " You, whom we are addressing, live in all ? parts of England; but everywhere, in the metropolis, in the manufacturing towns, and in the country, you sec about you the most pitiable destitution and degradation. In London there are, we understand, more than 1 ,000,000 of immortal beings who arc never seen in the house of God, and practically think the thoughts and live the lives of absolute heathens. The condition of a large portion of the labouring population of that vast city may be judged from the fact, that of its 20,000 journeymen tailors, 14,000 can barely earn a miserable subsistence by working 14 hours a day, Sunday included ; and that it contains 33,000 needle-women, who earn on an average only 4 l-2d. a day by working 14 hours. There

are 50,000 people in London who obtain their living in the streets; and Henry Mayhew, an authority whom ' you will not venture to question, says of them þÿ When the religious, moral, and intellectual degradation of the majority of these 50,000 people is impressed upon us, it becomes positively appalling to contemplate the vast amount of vice, ignorance, and want existing in the very heart of our land.' There are 30,000 costermongers ; of these he says þÿ ' Only onetenth þÿ at the outside one-tenth þÿ of the couples living together and carrying on their costcrinongering trade are married ;' that ' not three in a hundred of them hud ever been in the interior of a church or any place of worship, or knew what was meant by Christianity, and only one in ten of them is able to read.' In your manufacturing towns the case is no better. In Glasgow there are 60,000 women engaged in factories or needlework, whose average earnings do not exceed 7s. or 8s. a week. Dr. Patcrson, whom you know and respect as one of the most eminent divines in that city, stated in a public speech not long since, that in three wynds, constituting but a portion of his parish, there were, in a population of 3,232, only 83 church sittings, or little more than an average of 2 1-2 to 100; and that in the whole locality there were only 1 17 Bibles, ' Certain it is,' he exclaims, ' that nothing short of a levy en masse of whatever there is of living Christianity in the city, in all the branches of the Church of
Christ, will suffice to make head against tho augmenting ignorance, and ungodliness, and infi-

destroy the evil it will destroy us. Out of 10,461 burials in that city in 1850 no less than 2,381, or nearly a fourth, were at the public expenses. Glasgow in these particulars, is but a specimen of your manufacturing towns generally. So, too, of your country population . A very large number of your agricultural population live in filthy and crowded cottages, where the sexes arc in close and perilous contact night and day, where decency is difficult and comfort impossible ; the effect of which is to break down the barriers of morality, to obliterate all the sweet and saving attractions of a home, to weaken and desecrate all domestic ties, and to brutalise the manners and debase every natural feeling. The cottage accommodations of your villages is little or no better ; and the low tone of morality which this, in conjunction with other unfavourable influences, has caused may be inferred from the following sad state-
3 s

view : þÿ ment made last May in the North British Re- ' There are few things more remarkable in the sight of observant residents in many country villages than the small number of marriages solemnised in the course of the year. Among these few things, wc are afraid, roust be mentioned the number of illegitimate children that are born into the world. In some villages, indeed, these events are of such frequent occurrence as to excite neither surprise nor indignation There is something in this kind of insensibility which is very chilling and disheartening. This obtuseness of the moral senses, this deadness to shame, makes one almost despair over it. "When the standard of public opinion is so low, there is little hope of practical improvement.' " Now, sisters, we do not shut our eyes to the difficulties that might beset the sudden elevation of your degraded population to the rights and the dignity of manhood. But, nevertheless, we cannot be silent on those systems of your society which, in direct contravention of God's own law, deny in effect to the poor labourer the sanctity of marriage, with all its joys, rights, and obligations ; nor can wo be silent on that awful policy which, either by law, or by the absence of law, precludes any race of men, or any portion of the human family, from that education which alone can enable them to understand the truths of the Gospel and the ordinances of Christianity. We appeal to you as sisters, as wives, and as mothers, to raise your voices to your fellow citizens, and
your prayers to God, for the removal of England's shame from the Christian world." - þÿ H'i/mer Smith's European Timet, Feb. 16.

The following letter from the Earl of Shaftesbury appears in the London Times of Tuesday : þÿ Sir, þÿ A reply to my letter front Genoa, which you were so good as to insert, lias appeared in your paper of the 28th of last month, it contains no disproval of my statements j it is directed simply to argue and while wash the Fugitive Slave Law. Let us take a few lines descriptive of this terrible enactment from the speech of the Hon. CharlesSumner, one of those powerful intellects and noble hearts that have shone so brightly in our sister country þÿ a speech delivered in the Senate of the United States, August 26, þÿ1852: "The Slave Act," Says Mr. Sumner, "violates the Constitution antishocks the public conscienoe With modesty, and yet with firmness, let me add, sir, it offends against the Divine law. The good citizen, as he thinks of the shivering fugitive, guilty of no crime, pursued, hunted down like a beast, while praying for Christian help and deliverance ; and as he reads the requirements of this act, is filled with horror. Here is a despotic mandate, to aid and assist in the prompt and efficient execution of this law. Again, let me speak frankly. Not rashly would I set myself against any provision of law. This grave responsibility I should not lightly assume. But here the path of duty is clear. By the Supreme law, which commands me to do no injustice ; b y the comprehensive Christian law of brotherhood ; by the Constitution which I have sworn to support,

I am bound to disobey this act. Never, in any capacity, can I render Voluntary aid in its execuf'eat tion. Fains and penalties T will endure, but this can suffer,' was the exclamation of the author of wrong I will not do. ' I cannot obey, but the ' Pilgrim's Progress,' when imprisoned for disobedience to an earthly statute. Better suffer injustice than do if. Better be tho victim, than the instrument of wrong Better be even the poor slave, returned to bondage, than the unhappycommissioner." " Finally, for the sake of peace and tranquility, eeaae to shock the public conscience. Mindful of the lowly whom it pursues ; mindful of the good men perplexed by its requirements ; in the name of charity þÿ in the name of the Constitution, repeal this enactment totally, and without

delay. Be inspired by the example of Washing- ;jriety, Beware of the grdans of wounded Souls. ton ; be ' admonished by those words of oriental Oppress not to the utmost a single heart, for a solitary sigh has powep to overseta whole world !'" What noble eloquence ! Carry those noble words, Sir, by the vehicle of your almost universal paper, to the press of every country, and to the heart of every lias ever heard the Divine rule, " What- human being, man, woman, or child, who soever ye would that men should do unto you, do ye even so unto them." And yet we are to be told by your correspondent that this monstrous act of legislation is the bond of the Union, the basis of the Compromise, the security of the Confederation, the strength of America! Wc will not believe it. Who, born on this side of the Atlantic, would have þÿpresumed I say not to utter, but þÿ to imagine such a libel on the vigour arid virtue of the United States? What? is the greatness of such an empire; þÿ is the power of such political and social ordinances as have produced, almost in the infancy of the nation, a marvellous succession of statesmen, patriots, warriors, poets, divines, and men of science : þÿ is the restless spirit of enterprise among her citizens; þÿ are their singular skill, energy, and perseverance the true sourcesof their mighty dominion þÿ all dependent upon a statute to enable the Southern slaveholder to recapture miserable girls and heart-worn victims, and force them back to the sufferings
from wliich they had escaped? If this be true, Which it cannot be, the sun of America will never reach its meridian. I am, Sir, your obedient servant, Nice, Feb. 2. Shaftesbury.

English Misery versus American Slavery. þÿ In commenting on the recent response to the Staft'ordhouse ladies, Douglas Jerrold says "There can be no doubt that there is much truth in what Mrs. America is made to speak. But the moral destitution, the moral blackness of a thousand English outcasts do not make five hundred free negroes of as many slaves. Very true is it that we have wretched, wo-begone children in our alleys; that we have "illicit" costermongers; that our needlewomen have starved, or, at times anticipated death by a plunge from Waterloo-bridge ; true that there has been grinding misery in factories; misery unceasing, remorseless as the machinery once set at work. Count Otte Moltke has just expired, at the age of 83. lie was an honourable statesman, and filled many high posts, until, under Christian Vlll., he took leave, after the appointment of the Prince of Noer as governor of the Duchies. From the- Observer, London, January 23. NEGRO þÿSLAVERY THE WOMEN OF THE UNITED STATES v. THE WOMEN " To be or not to be ? þÿ OF ENGLAND. that is the question." "The women of the United States" ( sic in nrig. ) have just published an affectionate and Christian address "to their l isters the women of England," on the subject of negro slavery. This address is intended as a reply to the declaration of the ladies of this country, assembled some time since at Stafford House, on this much-vexed question, it will be remembered that the latter denounced in no measured terms the inhumanity and the unchristian system of slavery in the United States, and that it called upon the Americans by one mighty effort to make a sacrifice similar to that made by the people of England for the redemption of the negro race through all future time in the British dominions. The so-called reply of the women of the United States bears about it many marks of its masculine fabrication ; and indeed critically regarded it mdy be considered a clumsy forgery. In fact the only feature of probability it bears is the form of argument known as 7'» qnoque. Nevertheless, as it is a document of undoubted ability ; and as,

a <o 'jtt © a a a t a s moreover it realizes in respect to this country the individual wish of the Scottish hard þÿ " O that the Lord the gift would gie us To see ourselves as others see us," exhibiting freely many national defects, putting the finger on the tender places þÿ monstrare digito þÿ in some cases the plague sores, social probing and political, of the British people, to the quick, it is deserving at least, of a passing notice. It is true that Ireland is a poverty stricken degraded nation, as the sni disant address of the women of the United States says : it is true that Great Britain made war upon the Chinese, on the ground of the suppression of the flagitious opium traffic : it is true that poverty, hunger, " and dirt," to say nothing of vice, ignorance, and crime, prevail rich, in and powerful, and humane England." But that is no justification of negro slavery in America. Two wrongs do not make a right in morals, though two negatives may mean an affirmative in philology. And, therefore, even assuming crying sin against nature þÿ the worst as regards þÿ Slavery is altogether this country, that indefensible as regards America. This is one of t lie defects of the hi quoque mode of logic. Again, the fathers, the husbands, the brothers, the sons of the women of England, may have visited the immense aggregation of evils, adverted to by the document in question, upon every land where British arms have passed, or where British rule is paramount ; hut why should that fact, assuming it to be true, he held sufficient warranty

for the bondage, soul and body, of three millions of the coloured race iu America þÿ for the brutality of a Haley þÿ for the indifference of a St. Clair þÿ for the fiendish atrocity of a Legrcc r Taking it as granted, for the sake of the argument, that this question, however, arises, that " comes home to document is what it purports to he, another the business and bosoms" of the women of the United States of America in the matter. The most active partizans of the Anti-Slavery Society in England, when England was a slave-holding country, were The Women of England ;" with " them, indeed, may he said to have originated the abolition, movement, which reduced the fathers and husbands, and brothers and sons of many of tlieni from the almost fabulous opulence of a planter's life to a condition not of comparative but of absolute poverty ; they certainly were the best friends and most steadfast supporters of abolition ; and to their immortal honour be it said, they never relaxed in their efforts þÿ whether at home or abroad þÿ and made a free man þÿ until the negro was manumitted " liberated, elevated, disenthralled." It may have been a mistake on their parts specially to adopt the case of the negro to the partial exclusion of the social pariah, known as the white slave in the political slang of this country ; but that is their whole fault, and the good effected by them for the negro þÿ the real slave, contradistinguished as trom the constructive slave just adverted to is unquestioned and þÿ

unquestionable. Have the women of the United States effected any commensurate good for their suffering fellow-creatures, of any class, race, or condition in the new or iu the old world ? The answer is decidedly in the negative. The natu- j dridge, his brother-in-law, in regard to the neral, and indeed inevitable conclusion, therefore, | groes (thirty-three is, the same level of Immunity with the Women of that until they shall have placed " themselves on England," the women of the United States of America are not authorized, either in moral law or inexorable logic, so to speak, to assume the position of mentors in the matter under consideration. At the same time it must ho conceded that many of the facts adduced in the document under notice, are per sr. undeniable, and as such discreditable to the last degree to the national character of England. It cannot be denied that the land is filled with slaves þÿ slaves to ignorance, slaves to penury, slaves to vice ; nor that while no country in the world is richer, and no aristocracy Europe in arc prouder, no land exists where the poor arc more pauperised, more numerous in comparison witli the other classes, more irreligious (perhaps) and undoubtedly less educated. GENERAL WASHINGTON ON NEGRO SLAVERY. General Washington's opinion on the important question of slavery in the United States of America lias been entirely forgot, though with every American that opinion ought to have the weight of an overpowering authority. The following extracts from the general's will, not only establishes the principle of freedom and humanity, hut it also points out a safe and prudent mode of surmounting the supposed difficulties to be encountered in effecting a general emancipation. It is as follows : þÿ " Upon the demise of my wife, it is my will and desire that all the slaves which 1 hold iu my own right shall receive their freedom. To emancipate them during her life would, though earnestly wished by me, he attended with such insuperable difficulties, on account of their intermixture by marriages with the dower negroes, as to excite the most painful sensations, if not disagreeable consequences, from the latter, while both descriptions are in the occupancy of the same proprietor ; it not being in my power, under the tenure by which the dower negroes are held, to manumit them. And whereas among those who will receive freedom according to this demise, there may he some who, from old age or bodily Infirmities, and others who, on account of their infancy, will be unable to support themselves, it is my will and desire that all who come under the first and second description, shall he comfortably clothed and fed by my heirs while they live ; and that such of the latter description

as have no parents living, or if living are unable or unwilling to provide for them, shall he hound by the court till they shall arrive at the age of 2b years ; and in cases where no record can be produced whereby their age can bo ascertained, the judgment of the court, upon its own view of the subject, shall be adequate and final. The negroes thus hound are (by their masters or mistresses) to be taught to read and write, and to be brought up to some useful occupation, agreeably to the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia, providing for the support of orphan and other poor children. " Item : To the directors, governors, or by whatever denomination they may be designated, of the academy in the town of Alexandria, I give and bequeath (in trust) four thousaud dollars, or in other words, twenty of the shares which I hold in the Bank of Alexandria, towards the support of a free school, established at, and annexed to, the said academy, for the purpose of educating such orphan children, of such poor and indigent persons as are unable to accomplish it with their own means, and who, in the judgment of the trustees of the said seminary, are best entitled to the benefit of this donation, Ac., fyc., Ac." i Also, in reference to an estate which he settled for her life on Mary, widow of Bartholomew Dun-

crease), the general declares, in number, with their in- " It is my will and desire, that at the expiration her natural life, of j nil those who are forty years old and upwards, shall receive their freedom ; under that age, and above sixteen, shall serve seven years, and no longer ; mul all under sixteen years shall serve until I hey are twenty-five, and then to be free, fyc., ftc. " Signed, George Washington. "Dated 179 þÿ (omitted), and of the independence of the United States, the twenty-fourth." The tnode here prescribed, of gradually manumitting a large number of slaves (in all more than 900) is prudent and judicious, and would be still more requisite in the manumission of two or three millions of slaves. It would, indeed, remove every well-founded objection to that fulfilment of justice, humanity, and Christian duty. The great Washington could not die in peace, without securing emancipation to his own negro slaves ; and his illustrious successor, Jefferson, asserted the propriety, the safety, and advantage, both to the planter and to the nation at large, of a general emancipation. Must it he stated, that half a United century has elapsed, and the followed States have not yet republicans of the the precept and the example of those patriots who secured freedom, and bequeathed their glory to an unworthy generation ? But humanity and the love of liberty glow in the breast of American women. Warmed by the writings of a sister genius, their children will surely imbibe the noble inspiration,
and do honour to their country. þÿ lb. To the honour of Mrs. Washington, let it be remembered, that she did not let thein wait for her demise, but gave freedom to all her slaves in her lifetime.

From the New York " Albion ." WILL of the DL'KE of ORLEANS. From the original found at the village of the Chateau des Tuileries, on the 24th of Feb. 1848. The following document appeared in the last number of the Revue du Nouvean Monde, and struck us as being well worth translating. It exhibits, indeed, the character of Louis Philippe's eldest son, the late Duke of Orleans, under the most favourable point of view ; for if his political aspirations are but vaguely defined herein, his strong affections, confiding disposition, and lofty tone of feeling, stand out in singularly strong colours. The evident restraint under which he speaks of the King will not escape notice ; nor can it be wondered at, when we consider the Father as the personification of craft and selfishness, and the son as adding to his many accomplishments a loyal, frank, and generous spirit. At the date borne by that testament, the Duke was about to embark for Africa, where his military services will be remembered. His untimely death þÿ not on the battle field þÿ not from perils of the sea þÿ but by a fall from his carriage þÿ took place little more than two years later, and was, indeed, a heavy calamity for France. The noble woman, to whom he here expresses himself so devotedly attached, and in whom he places such implicit confidence, was, so far as we can judge, in every way worthy of his choice. Her spirited behaviour during the trying scenes of the Revolution of February 1848, will not be, and ought not to be forgotten. " If the sacred duty I am about to ful-

fil is to be the conclusion of a career not brilliant, but without spot, I feel assured that my whole family will only see in this expression of my last wishes a further mode of testifying the affection and gratitude which pervade my heart, by furnishing to all related to me, when I shall be no longer in their midst, the means ofrealizingsome of thosethouglits which I shall have borne away with inc. But before pointing out these wishes, which I do not perhaps here trace in a legal form, knowing that amongst ourselves such a precaution would be needless, I feel the necessity of offering my respectful acknowledgment to the King who has always heen so good to me, to the Queen to whom I owe so much, and to my aunt, who has invariably treated me as a son. "Although I am certain that my family, whose indissoluble unanimity, I will know, will do for me that which in similar cases I would have done for every member of it, and will look upon themselves as intimately associated with my affection for my beloved llelen, yet I venture to believe that by again recommending to the King, to the Queen, to my brother Nemours, to my aunt, and to all my brothers and sisters, one who has rendered me happy, I shall establish a further tie between her and my family, of which I flatter myself she will in every way partake the destiny. "I feel confident that even though her duties towards the children I have left her, should no longer bind her to the fate of my family, the remembrance of

him who has loved her more than every thing in this world, would associate her with all the various chances of our future fate and with the cause we serve. Helen knows my ardent and positive wishes upon this head, and knows what I should suffer, were I to believe her in another camp than that in which arc all my present sympathies, in which all my duties have lain. It is this confidence, hitherto so fully justified by the noble character, the elevated mind and perfect

<o st ® it £ devotedness of Helen, that causes me to desire that she should remain exclusively entrusted with the education of our children. " But I hasten to add that, if unfortunately the authority of the King cannot watch over my eldest son until he shall have attained his majority, Helen should not allow her name to be put forward for the regency, and should loudly disavow any attempt, which might be concealed under this dangerous pretext, at depriving my brother Nemours or in his default the eldest of my brothers, of the Regency. " By leaving as is her duty and her interest, all the cares of the government in virile hands and those accustomed to wield the sword, II elen could devote herself entirely to the education of her children, as she has devoted herself hitherto to me. " It is a great and difficult task to prepare the Count of Paris for the destiny which awaits him, for no one can foretell, at the present time, what that child will be, when the occasion shall arise for reconstructing upon new foundations a society, which is now supported only by the ruins, mutilated and ill assorted, of its preceding organization. But whether the Count of Paris be one of those instruments, broken before they have been used, or become one of the labourers in that social regeneration of which we can now but have a glimpse through great obstacles and perhaps through streams of blood ; whether he be King, or whether he remains an unknown and obscure defender of a cause to which we all belong, he

must be, above all, a man of his age, and of the nation ; he must be a Catholic, and the impassioned and exclusive servant of France and of the Revolution. "I am certain that, although remaining personally faithful to her owh religious convictions, Helen will scrupulously bring up our children in the religion of their father, in that religion which in all ages France has professed and defended, and the pri nciple of which is so perfectly in accordance with the new social ideas, to whose triumphs my son is bound to consecrate himself. " Without being able or willing to trace out before-hand a plan of education for my son, I will here indicate some leading points in the course to be pursued. I hold it important that he should at an early age commence the study of foreign languages, and subsequently that of history, which he should be made seriously and thoroughly to investigate. " Elegant accomplishments should only occupy him as accessories, especially whilst he shall be sharing the public education of his contemporaries. I hope that before that time a serious reform will have taken place in college education, which shall place it more in harmony with the equipments of society. But be that as it may, I formally demand that my son be subjected to this trial of public instruction, which in an age where there is no other possibly hierarchy than that of intelligence and energy, can alone insure the complete development of these two qualifications. I desire even, without wishing that my son

should enter the Fcole Poly technique, that he should undergo the public examination necessary for admission to that school. When he shall commence his career and his military labours, let him first serve in the Infantry, in that branch which for so many ages has been the national service of Frenchmen, and in the ranks of which the whole people ought to enrol themselves, on the day when any attempt shall be made to execute against France, against her wishes, and the dynasty, the sentence long pronounced against these illustrious non-

appearants. " But that which I recommend above all things to my dear Helen, that for which I also much rely upon the Queen, is the moral direction to be given to the education of my son, the impressions which he will not find in books, nor in the lessons of his masters, but which cannot be given at too early an age. "Helen knows that my political faith is even dearer to me than my religious standard. My convictions, being after my affections, what 1 cling to most dearly of all in this world, I sincerely wish to bequeath them to my son þÿ not from the foolish pride of believing myself infallible, but from a profound and deeply considered sentiment of fidelity. It is moreover the only inheritance that I can leave to my son, not having a fortune to transmit to him, nor a name, that I have myself acquired, nor a sword of which I have made use. But I will leave to him what is better than all this : I will leave to him that which should most inspire an elevated soul þÿ great duties to fulfil, and immense obstacles to surmount in order to fulfil them. " When bequeathing to him the defence of a country and of a threatened principle, I sought to bequeath to him at the same time, faith in their good right and their final triumph. Let these thoughts and this devotedness, which have died in me without heing applied, germinate in the heart of my son ; let him in his affection for France always know how to be her accomplice and never her keeper ; let him think only of his ancestors, to feel how much the

greatness of his race adds to the extent of his duties. Let him be taught that he belongs to the first family in the world, but for the purpose of rendering him proud and worthy of one day holding in his hands the destiny of the most glorious cause which after Christianity, has heen pleaded before mankind ; let him be the apostle of that cause, and should it be necessary, its martyr. " And this is what Helen should also repeat to my second son, if it he a son 1o whom she is soon to give birth ; should it be so, without expressing a decided will, I must say that I have sometimes thought of giving to this child the name of Robert Philippe, and of begging the King to grant him the title of Prince of Algiers. If, on the contrary, I should become the father of a girl, I wish that she may have the names of Marie Amelie Auguste Helen, and that on the day of her birth the book of prayers which 1 have had made should be presented to her, to which it remains only to add the arms and the escutcheons. " I now proceed to the disposal of the property which belongs to me. I have neither debts nor hoardings. Possessing only a life annuity, I have no fortune to leave my children ; the only things of which 1 can dispose are moveables ; I leave all my paintings, arms, and articles of art, to the Count of Paris, saving the exceptions pointed out herein. If after having liquidated my accounts, there should be found some louisin my coffer, I desire that this sum, whatever it may be, should he employed in purchasing

an annuity for Helen. I know that she will estimate it, not by the value, hut by the intention. Should it become necessary to sell a portion of my carriages or my horses, the produce of such sale should also be added to the capital I wish to leave to my dear Helen. (To be continued.) runs thus þÿ This sentence is somewhat obscure. The original " le jour ou l'on tentera d' executer contre la France, contre les idees et la dynastie, la sentence depnis long-temps renduc contre ces illustres contumaccs." Docs the Duke in this last expression intimate that tha political system of his day had been tried and condemned at the bar of public opinion, though refusing to appear and plead there ? On whose behalf should arms be taken up? þÿ Ed. Ab.

This wonderful vessel, tlie success of which is exciting so much attention among all classes at home and abroad, went down tlie bay yesterday, on another trial trip, having made wlmt is called an þÿ engineer þÿtrip s some days back. This second trip was determined on to dispel, by another occitlar demonstration, the evil reports that, in

been raised against the practicability of the experiment. Accordingly a party of about sixty invited guests, composed of members of the press and several scientific gentlemen, assembled on board a towboat, at Whitehall, at nine þÿo clock, from which they were transferred to the Ericsson, which was waiting for visitors in the North River, off Pier No. 1 . At half-past nine exactly the first turn of the wheels was made. At fifteen minutes to ten site was abreast the fort on Govþÿeruor I s sland, and reached Fort Diamond at exactly fifteen minutes to eleven þÿo clock, a distance of about seven miles and a-lialf, against a strong head wind and tide. When between þÿGovernor s Vive þÿKossuth. þÿ Island and Quarantine the steam -ship tialtie , from Liverpool, was passed, which saluted us with cannon, and several hearty rounds of cheers, which were promptly returned. After the Ericsson had proceeded about a mile and a-lialf below tlie Narrows she was put about, and returned to the city, arriving at her starting point in tlie North River at a quarter past twelve. The distance from þÿGovernor Island s to her turning point and back was about eighteen miles, which was accomplished in two hours and a-lialf. The greatest number of revolutions made on the trip was ten and a quarter, and the greatest speed attained was at the rate of nine miles an hour. This trip was not made to show her speed, but to convince Ihe public that tlie parties interested in her have succeeded in their promise of proving

the capability of a vessel being propelled by calorie. On the way back the party assembled in the saloon, when Captain Ericsson explained, by the aid of a diagram, tlie whole principle and method of working his caloric engines. He gave a succinct history of the whole matter, and demonstrated the method by which the atmosphere was drawn in cold, then forced through a wire network, forming a surface of ir>,000 square inches, into a lower cylinder, where, receiving additional heat from the furnace, it expanded in the larger cylinder so as to raise it, and then, when it had done its work, it escaped through the work of wire gauze into the open air, having imparted the greater portion of its heat to the wire work, which was again absorbed by the fresh draft of cold air passing through the same wire meshes to l>e heated. There are four double cylinders, set perpendicularly and longitudinally to the boat, two abaft and two forward of the main wheel shaft. They all move in connexion, those forward rise, while those in tlie rear of the shaft sink. There are two pistons or driving crank rods, which turn the wheel shafts. One. is moved by a walking beam, which is moved by the cylinders in front, and the other by a similar beam in tire rear They both work on the same : crank of the wheel shaft, and at inclined angles, rising from below, in the form of the letter V, inverted thus, \, with the shaft crank for botli at the apex. Hence, while one rod is pushing the other is pulling the crank, thus avoiding the dead

point, usually encountered in the ordinary crank motions of steam engines, Ac . The pressure was uniformly at twelve pounds to the square inch. Captain Ericsson estimated the force of his machinery at, BOO horse-power The upper cylinder

in each ease contained a head surface of 14,000 square inches, and the lower cylinders a surface of 22,000 square inches. The diameters of the main cylinders were about 168 inches. The main valves were about two feet in diameter. The consumption of coal was at the rate of about six tons in twenty-four hours. During Capt. Ericsþÿson lucid s exposition of his machinery, he invited the most rigid scrutiny and investigation. Many questions were put by parties present, which he answered with great clearness and promptness One question asked regarded the packing of the cylinders, which it had been said would melt and let the air escape. He showed that, by filling the cylinder heads with non-conducting materials, and the packing by surrounding the head, being above the surface exposed to heated air, was kept cool. He also showed how a man, by standing on a cylinder head, could, by hand, readily lubricate every part of the surface of the cylinder. The packing, also, he showed to be at all times in command of the engineer or attendant, which was not the ease in steam engines. To a ques lion regarding the oxidization, expansion and construction of tlie iron composing the bottoms of the main cylinders immediately over the fires in the furnaces, he stated that the iron composing them was an inch and a quarter thick, and when they gave out, which would not be over once in five years, new ones could immediately be substituted without displacing any of the machinery; and, were it desirable to make them endure for a

longer period, they could have their surfaces exposed to the fire coated with firebriek clay. He said they did not expand, or contract, or vibrate but very little, and not more than was common to metal similarly used in other engines. Many other questions were put and answered, regarding tlie backing or reversing the action of his machinery, and when stopping her on her course for an hour, more or less, lmw he would start her again. To the latter question he said, if the detention exceeded many minutes, he would start just as he would in the first instance, by pumping a supply of fresh air, which would soon become expanded in the large cylinder, and put all in motion. But a pressure of half-a-pound to the square inch would start the engine, and the weight of the crank alone was sufficient to put it in motion. Tlie expense of running a caloric engine, he stated, would be but one-fifth of that of a steam-engine of the same power. In conclusion, Captain Ericsson stated that he was induced to go on this trial trip for tlie sake of the parties interested with him ; but, as to himself, he had all along been perfectly satisfied of tlie successful issue of the experiment ; and, owing to the machinery not being tight., which is a thing only to he accomplished by degrees, the engines were not working much more than ouc-half of their power, but that, tlie trial had fully answered his expectations, and he was confident that the principle would in a short time he universally adopted

So clear were Captain þÿEricsson s explanations, that he was urged to give a lecture at the Metropolitan-hall, illustrated, as yesterday by his model, on a larger scale, which we trust that he will do. It was conceded by all that Captain Ericsson had demonstrated his success in establishing, beyond all doubt, a new principle of motive power, and that all that was wanted was its pro per application to the great end intended. All that is necessary to gain additional power is to increase the diameter of the cylinders. Those in the present ship, it is clear, are too small to give the power and speed that are desirable. Captain Ericsson said he foresaw this difficulty, but was told by ironfounders that, they Could not cast the cylinder of greater dimensions than fourteen feet. Since these were made up that size, and put in this ship, a firm in New York has offered to guarantee to cast them of twenty feet in diameter. Captain Ericggon estimates that were the present þÿship cylinders s of sixteen feet diameter, she would make a speed equal to the best oceau steamers, or twelve to fourteen miles per hour ; and that a vessel with twenty feet cylinders would outstrip the speed of anything that now floats on the water. Captain Ericsson thinks the principle can be modified to propel locomotives on railroad.', and applied to nearly all kinds of stationary work, great and small. A locomotive on this plan Could be made to traverse a street, without stopping for water or fuel on the way

A meeting wa« subsequently organized, at which resolutions Were adopted, congratulating Captain Ericsson on the success of his great experiment, and expressing conviction that the invention is no longer of questionable practicability, but from this day takes rank with the foremost of the great and useful inventions which the world owes to science and genius, and that it promises to surpass, in efficiency, any other adjunct to the advancement, of commerce and Ihe industrial pro gross of the world þÿ

The Vienna correspondent of the London Times, writing on the 20th says: þÿ Up to the year 1818, the connexion between the Austrian Sovereigns and their subjects was of a much more intimate nature than is customary in other countries. Audiences were given once, and even twice, a week by the different emperors, to all applicants, and individuals who fancied themselves wronged by the authorities invariably laid their grievances before and demanded redress from their "Kaiser." The consequence of this continual and direct eomuiunication between the monarch and the people was that a " patriarchal connexion" was established. A mutual sympathy existed. Unfortunately, the. revolution destroyed the harmony which had so long existed in the great family. The monarch lost confidence in his subjects, and the latter became more and more estranged from their natural friend and protector. The Severn steamer arrived at Southampton on Thursday with advices front Jluenos Ayres to the 2nd of January, llio Janeiro to the 14th, and Lisbon to the loth instant. The news front Buenos Ayres is of a most unfavourable character. A new revolution having taken place, a fresh provisional government was installed, and civil war immediately broke out, and continued up to the date of the sailing of the packet. The following is an extract from letter dated Buenos Ayres, .lau. 2 : " December a private has been a stirring month for our good city. On the 1st a revolution broke out, headed by the Minister of M ar As a dislike to the person of Governor Alsina was the only motive assigned, he disinterestedly and patriotically resigned, thinking thereby to allay the tempest. This point conceded, new demands were preferred, anil it soon became evident that the first object was to levy a heavy contribution on the capital, and then seize the government, falling back on the assistance of Urquiza, if necessary. To this last condition very few in the city were willing to accede, and accordingly we have another new government, and the revolution still continues ; the town closely besieged by the gauchos ; all business at a dead standstill; beef, the staff of life with a large proportion of the community, at 40 or. 50 times its usual price ; and almost daily skirmishes in the neighbourhood of the city and in the lanes of the outskirts. Every native is or ought to ho a soldier ; and many foreigners, from instinct or

sympathy, lend their aid for the defence of the capital. We consider the triumph secure in the first instance, but should the rebels be allowed to retreat to the north and form a junction with Urquiza, it may occasion a serious complication. We have very recent news from the capital of Paraguay. Sir Charles Hotham had arrived there, hut matters were not going on very smoothly with the foreign diplomatists. It is reported to-day that a son of the President of Paraguay has arrived here, supposed to be on a special mission. We should not be surprised to bear that the Paraguayans embrace the cause of Buenos Ayres. Their commercial interests may suggest and would amply justify that policy An official proclamation has just been issued, announcing the approach to the city of Colonel Pedro Rosas y Belgrano, at the head of 5,000 men, in support of the Pro-

A 11 F.ltOlN'E AT THE DIGGINGS. þÿ The Diihlin Commercial Journal publishes a letter of quite a romantic character, lately received by a lady of Dublin from a young female friend, and former schoolfellow of hers, now tit the Australian diggings. It appears from her narrative that she and her brother were suddenly left orphans with <£300 for their necessities, and all the fancies and nicities is which life in prosperous circumstances wont to include. " lie had passed through college with credit, and could write poetry and ride up to the hounds as well ;ts any huntsman who ever hunted the Golden Vale, while I, on my part, could play polkas, sing ballads, speak French and a little German, was a capital horsewoman (only I had no horse), and once in my life had composed a waltz, and written Hi chapters of a novel, which broke down from my not knowing how to get my heroine out of a terrible scrape. Hut, alas! my dear friend, all enough these ' once things might upon a have time,' done hut well the real battle of life was now to he fought by two utterly inexperienced raw recruits, and the question was, how our time and means were to In profitably rather than pleasantly spent. Fortunately, we were both young, strong, active, and hearty, and never did any Sebastian and Viola of them all love each other with a stronger and more enduring affection than did Frank and 1 þÿ sole remnants, as we were, of so much prosperity and so little prudence." the After much nervous consultation over £300,

they determined to emigrate to Australia. <Jn reaching Melbourne they found that they could not encounter worse inconveniences at the diggings, and there they now are under singularly interesting circumstances. The young lady says: þÿ "I was resolved to accompany my brother and his friends to the diggings, and I felt that to do so in my own proper costume and character would he to run unnecessary hazard. Hence my change. I cut my hair into a very masculine fashion ; 1 purchased a broad felt hat, a sort of tunic or smock of coarse blue cloth, trousers to conform, hoots of a miner, and thus parting with my sex for a season (I hoped a belter one), behold me an accomplished candidate for mining operations and all the perils and inconveniences they might he supposed bring. to All this transmutation took place with Frank and Mr. M 's sanction; indeed, it was he who first suggested the change, which I grasped at and improved on. I could not I ear to lie separated from Frank, and we all felt that I should he safer in my male attire than if I exposed myself to the dangers of the route and residence in my proper guise. We have now been nine weeks absent from Melbourne and have tried three localities, at Ihe latter of which we have been most fortunate. We are near water (a first rate article), and our tent is pitched on the side of as pretty a valley as you could wish to visit. 1 have for myself a sort ol 'supplementary canvas chamber,' in which 1 sleep, cook, wash clothes þÿ that is, my own and

Frank's þÿ and keep watch and ward over heaps of gold dust arid ' nuggets,' the sight and touch of which inspirit me when I grow dull, which 1 seldom do, for I have constant 'droppers in', and to own the truth, even in my palmiest days I never was treated with greater courtesy or respect. Of course, my sex is gene- rally known. I am called ' Mr. Harry' (an abbreviation of Harriet); hut no one

intrudes the more on that account. In fact, I have become a sort of 'necessity,' as I am always ready to do a good turn þÿ t lie great secret, after all, of social success ; and I never refuse to oblige a ' neighbour,' be the trouble what it may. The consequences are pleasant enough. Many a 'nugget' is thrust on me whether I will or no, in return for cooking a pudding or darning a shirt, and if all the cooks and semstresses in the world were as splendidly paid as I am the 'Song of the Shirt' would never have been written, at all events. My own hoard amounts now to about 10 lb. of gold, and if I go on accumulating, even the richest heiress in my family in former days will lie left immeasurably behind. Sometimes, when 1 have a few idle hours, I accompany Frank and his comrades to the diggings, and it is a rare thing to watch the avidity with which every ' bucket' is raised, washed, examined, and commented upon. Wild the life is, certainly, but full of excitement and hope; and, strange as it is, I almost fear to tell you, that I do not wish it to end! You can hardly conceive what a merry company gather together in our tent every evening, or how pleasantly the hours pass. Tea and coffee we have in plenty, for every one brings a hoard, and milk we manage to obtain, for among us we have imported two cows, which cost us about £50 each, hut that is a mere trifle. Cake of various kinds I manufacture, thanks to old Betsy D for teaching me; and as for liquor, we sometimes have a little wine, brandy,

or arrack, and sometimes not. And then we dance to the music of a German flute, played by a real German, or we sing glees and quartctts, or talk of Moore, Byron, Burns, Goethe, 'Shakspeare and the musical glasses,' &c., until midnight, and sometimes long after it. As to suitors, 1 have them in plenty, and not despicable ones either, I assure you."-lb.

When you get the money you must come at once, whatever your position at home may be, for hero something worth having is to be made, þÿ that is all !" þÿ Ibid

Accounts from the French capital announce the opening of the Legislative Assembly, by the Emperor, who delivered a speech, which had caused a lavorable impression both on the Paris Bourse and on the London Stock Exchange, owing to the Emperor's expressed declaration of a pacific line of policy, and of a reduction ot the army to the extent of 20,000 men. The following is the emperor'S speech. Senators and Deputies þÿ A year since I called you together in this place to inaugurate the constitution promulgated in virtue of the powers which the people had conferred on me. Since that period calm has not been disturbed. The law, in resuming its sway, has allowed the return to their homes of the majority of the men who were made the subject of necessary severity. The riches of the nation have increased to such a point that that portion of our floating capital, the value of which can be estimated, amounts to about two millions. The activity of labor devclopcs itself in every branch of industry. The same progress isbeing realized in Africa, where our army has just distinguished itself by heroic successes. The form of the government has been changed, without any shock, by the free suffrages of the people. Great works have been undertaken without the creation of any new tax, and without a loan. Peace has been maintained without weakness. All the powers have recognized the new government. France has now institutions which can defend themselves, and the stability

of which does not depend on the life of one man. The results have not cost great efforts, because they were in the minds and for the interest of all. To those who would doubt their importance, 1 will reply that scarcely fourteen months ago, France was delivered up to the hazards of anarchy. To those who may regret that a wider field has not been given to liberty, I will reply, that liberty has never aided in founding a durable political edifice; it crowns it when it has been consolidated by time, Let us, besides, not forget that the immense majority of the country has confidence in the present, and faith in the future ; there still remain incorrigible individuals, who, forgetful of their own experience, of their past terrors, and of their disappointments, obstinately persist in paying no attention to the national will, deny the reality of facts, and in the midst of a sea which everyday grows more and more calm call for tempests in which they would be the first to be swallowed up. These occult proceedings of the different parties serve no purpose but to show their weakness; and the government, instead of being disturbed at them, only thinks of governing France, and tranquillizing Europe. For this double object it has the firm determination to diminish expenses and armament, and to devote to useful purposes all the resources of the country, to keep up with good faith international relations, in order to prove to the most incredulous that when France expresses herformal in-

tention to remain at peace, it may be believed, for she is strong enough not to deceive any one. You will see, gentlemen, by the budget which will be presented to you, that our financial position has never been better for the last twenty years, and that the public revenue has increased beyond all provisions. Nevertheless, the effective force of the army, already reduced by 30, (MR) men in the course of the last year, is about to be immediately reduced by 20,000 more.

<B 1R <8> I 3L A x? 1 j The majority of the laws which will be presented to you will not go beyond necessary exigencies, and that is the most favorable indication of our situation. The people are happy when governments do not find it necessary to resort to extraordinary measures. Let us, therefore, thank Providence for the visible protection which it has accorded to our efforts ; let us persevere in this course of firmness and moderation, which reassures without irritating ; which leads to good without violence ; and so prevents all reaction. Let us always i reckon on God and on ourselves ; as on the mutual support which we owe to ourselves ; and let us be proud to see in so short a time this great country pacified, prosperous at home, and honored abroad. At the meeting of the Legislative body on the 15th, the President, M. Billault, announced that he had received from M. Bouhir a letter conceived in terms so improper that he considered it his duty to abstain from reading it in public. " M. Bouhir," he said, " is free to give in his resignation ; but it is not permitted that he should protest against the will of the nation and the constitution." M. Bouhir exclaimed against the interpretation ascribed to his words, but the President ordered him to be silent, and declared that if during the next fifteen days he had not taken the oath required by the constitution, he should be considered as having resigned. After this incident the Assembly rose. The Monitcur of Paris publishes the following article (supposed to be from

the pen of the Emperor himself,) on the pamphlet entitled " Letters Franques." It will be seen that the sanguinary longings of the writer of the pamphlet, which caused so much uneasiness in England, are entirely disavowed by the French government : þÿ Parties cannot accustom themselves to see France and Europe escape from their hands. The peace of the world is onerous to them. Not daring to hope anything more from the public spirit, abused for a moment, their only hope is in tiie return of disorder. For that all means are good to them ; on one hand, sanguinary provocations ; on the other, anonymous calumnies, writings which, under pretext of awakening the generous instincts of the country, only tend to lead them astray, and to keep up by those means distrust and agitation. Such is the subject of a new pamphlet, entitled "Lettrcs Franeais," published by a writer of the legitimist party, and which would no more merit the attention of the government than of the public if there was not reason to believe that silence would be falsely interpreted. The author addresses himself, sans fa eon , to the Emperor of the French ; he decides with an incredible self-sufficiency on the highest diplomatic question and the destinies of Europe. After having taken for the motto of his pamphlet " the memorable words of the speech at Bordeaux, The empire is peace," the author only applies himself to urge France to war by holding up to its resentment established treaties, and endeavoring to revive an ancient hatred against England.

The tactics of those who inspire such publications are not difficult to be understood. They said to themselves that the government of the Emperor would be placed in the disagreeable alternative, either of wounding the national feeling by combating these writings, or by its silence giving them a sort of tacit approval which should be for Europe a permanent cause of disquietude and distrust. It is so painful for the vanquished parties to see peace and the general prosperity established without them and in spite of them. The snare is of too gross a kind for the country and the government to be caught in it. The Emperor as well as France, wishes for peace þÿ a fruitful, honorable peace, the only one which becomes the nation; and certainly it is not to the old parties that the heir of Napoleon the Great will go to ask counsel about national honor and dignity. One cannot feel too much surprised at such provocations pro-

ceeding from those who entertain legitimist opinions. l)o those writers believe, then that France has forgotten her recent history, and do they not know that it would be easy to confound them with it ? But the government has too much at heart the interest and the glory of the country, it considers the cessation of our ancient dissensions of too much importance to allow itself to have recourse to recrimination, even the best founded, by reviving melancholy recollections.

The Italian States. Milan is now reported quiet þÿ but the theatres, and public assemblages are prohibited. No outbreak bad occurred in the Tuscan or Roman States, except some rioting at Orvieto, where one man was stabbed and some windows broken. At Sienna and Rimini cries of " Viva la France" and " Viva Napoleon" were uttered, for which heavy fines were inflicted, and fifty persons were beaten with fifty blows each. At Monsea, six leagues from Milan, the insurgents held out bravely for some hours, but were overpowered. The expectations that the Hungarians in the Austrian army .would join the insurgents were totally misplaced. It is said that the Austrian police had known all about the conspiracy since the 10th of January last. The Times correspondent learns from a sure source that the rising in Italy was to be simultaneous with the assassination of Louis Napoleon. At a meeting of the conspirators at Lugano, on the 5th, news was received that the assassination plan had failed, and it quite discomfited the Italian revolt. It is said that ten thousand muskets are secreted at Lugano. The frontiers are still kept by a strong force of Piedmontese cavalry, and all refugees have been removed from Sardinia to the north side of lake Maggie. General Castellane, at Lyons, announced that if disturbances occurred in Savoy, he would cross the . frontier with troops. Milan itself is in a sad state. Debtor prisoners are liberated to make room for political ones. The municipality is forced to pension the widows of soldiers and

the wounded troops; and house owners have been ordered to repair damages at their own expenses. Numerous public buildings are occupied by troops. Most of those arrested belong to the lowest orders of the people. Agostine denies, in the London papers, that he assented to the insurrection. Mazzini is somewhere in Switzerland or Italy, and his friends fear for his safety. It is generally understood that when Ilis Excellency Governor Feddersen received his appointment to these Islands, he stipulated permission to retire, if he considered it desirable, at the expiration of two years. This period being nigh at hand, it will, we are certain, be received as welcome tidings by the inhabitants generally, that, at the desire of the Home Government, His Excellency has consented to prolong his stay a year longer. Many among us have expressed much surprise that the members of the Colonial Assembly did not avail themselves of the suggestion of the Committee on the first draft of the Colonial Law, to moot and deprecate the principle of so short a term being alloted to fill a situation of so much importance ; þÿ two years being barely sufficient to induct the Governor in our local relations, þÿ consequently, just when his services might benefit the Colonies, another should displace him J-c. 4-c., ad infinitum þÿ an admirable plan, certainly, of making þÿ confusion worse þÿconfounded. That Governor Feddersen, therefore, has consented to prolong his stay among us is desirable and þÿgratifying desirable from the reasons above stated, and gratifying from his having gained the eonfidcnce of all intelligent members of the community, evincing, as he has done, an integrity of purpose and much firmness of character ; besides which a prolonged stay of his amiable and courteous Lady will continue to afford a moral picture of domestic happiness, highly bene-
ficial þÿ all of which are in strong contrast, þÿ but comparisons, it is said, are odious, and therefore refrain making any.

Official error is one of those evils that few communities can be said to be securely guaranteed against, but we hardly ever heard of a community which has been so seriously exposed to danger and calamity, by official error, as has been our case within the present week. It is not a triviai. circumstance that will arouse a population to so formal a remonstrance against authority, as the subjoined Memorial to our Chief in the Danish Antilles energetically puts forth. The case complained of was one of confluent SMALL POX, and the body of the patient, who died the day after ho was brought on shore, could not have been removed had the disease been known to the men employed to do so, such is the horror entertained in this Island for Small Pox, after what the inhabitants endured in 1843. " Shipley," on careening Island, A year or two ago there was a small building, kept, purposely for patients arriving here with Small Pox ; why this has been abandoned, and if abandoned, why another place, unconnected with the town, has not been substituted, those clothed in authority should be respectfully invited to explain : þÿ To His Excellency II. The Memorial of the undersigned Inhabitants of St. Thomas, complaining of a case of Small Pox having been admitted on arrival in this port from New York, by the Health Officer, into this town.

May it please Your Excellency. the Biitish brig " Iris" arrived in this port from The Memorial shews that on the 20th instant, New York, and on being boarded by the Officer in charge of the Harbour, tlio captain reported a case of Small Pox on board. The captain was ordered to hoist the quarantine flag, which he did,

arid on the case being reported to the King's Physician, this official repaired on board. The captain desired him to direct what should be done with the sick person, who had the disease in a very advanced state, when the King's Physician ordered to have him carried to the Hospital. The King's Physician then went together with the captain on shore, who communicated to his consignees what had happened ; the latter, not thinking it likely that the sick man was to be brought into this town, sent to ascertain of the King's Physician about the matter, when they were told by him that the sick man was to be carried to the Land-Kasscn Hospital, situated in this town ; whither he was consequently removed, and the vessel and crew admitted without any restriction to free intercourse with the town. Your Memorialists arc of opinion that by bringing the sick person into the town it has been exposed to the great peril of being infected by one of the most dreadful diseases known, and which some years ago carried away a large number of its inhabitants, and had at the same time the most detrimental influence on the intercourse and commerce with the neighbouring Islands, which were brought to a stand still for several months while the dreadful scourge v.as raging here. Your Memorialists have brought the case now in question to the knowledge of the Burgher Council, who they hope will investigate the matter, and report on it to the proper authorities. They look, however, to Your Excellency for im-

mediate aid, and they approach you with the humble prayer, to take at once measures as will make it impossible that the Health Officer act henceforth in similar or like eases in the same way he has judged proper to do in this, which your Mcmoriuli.-ts consider a rockh ss exposure of ho inhabitants of tlii- place, and their interests to the ravages of a disease dreadful in its consequences, by the very officer who is appoint d by Government to watch over the sanitary slate of the Island, and to take proper measures to protect it from contagious sickness being carried into its midst from foreign countries. They complain of the course of action the Health Officer adopted in this case, and trust that Your Excellency will promptly relieve your Memorialists' minds by taking such measures which Your Excellency may think proper to prevent a repetition of a case which naturally has caused great inquietude in this place. We have the honor to be, Your Excellency's most Obedient and humble servants, Here follow 121 signatures St. Thomas, 22nd Feb., 185.1.
