The Colonial Council beg leave here to insert the vote of a minority consisting of five members : This minority cannot unconditionally recommend those special sums proposed in the draft sub Chapter II. B and C., nor can it coincide with the amendments because does not think it advisable to proposed it to the same by the majority; fix permanently for the judicial offices in St. Croix and St. Thomas and the officials belonging thereto, sums to the amount proposed ; and because it does not deem it advisable that the office of a local chief magistrate in St. Thomas should be abolished. It is not advisable to regulate permanent public institutions, þÿ the worth of which does depend, not upon Rubrics and Salaries, but upon their organisation and other conditions, þÿ in making a general estimate of Revenue and Ex- þÿ penditure for a certain financial year. In the present instance it appears unsettled, not only how the functions of the judicial and police-establishments ought to be divided, but partly, in what they are to consist, and what, in means of action þÿ such as : officers, police-soldiers, horses þÿ will be wanted and can be obtained; and how it is to be secured, that all of it will give returns corresponding to the outlay. As long as such matters be unsettled and with such a meagre budget, which at all events does

not promise any surplus, it does appear advisable, not to bind yourself more than necessary, especially with regard to the details. þÿ When once we have caused the acceptance of the items of expense for the judicial and police-establishment, either of the bill laid before us, or of the report recommended by the majority, probably it will be too late to demand reductions and reforms ; it should be remembered, that there is no great probability that the credits of the budget will be more favorable in the first years to come ; and that the landtreasuries of St. Croix and St. John arc so badly off, that even without incurring new expenses, we may tear that they will require new taxes. But the number and the outward independence of the officials in question and their assistants are but one condition for an effective administration oflaw in these islands ; another and more important condition is, that these laws and particularly those legal forms, through which it works, and for the application of which payment is made, do correspond to the actual requirements of the people ; but such has hitherto not been the case, the more so, because those requirements must necessarily larger be shortly after a social commotion like

the emancipation, than with an ordinary state of things. The number of civil eases is very small, of larger estates but few are administered by the dealing-courts, but the large mass of the judicial cases, þÿ not to mention many cases, which ought to come before the courts, are not brought before them, þÿ are about disorders, assaults, injuries, larceny &c., great crimes are as yet of rare occurrence. On the treatment of that class of cases and on the results of such treatment depends, not alone the general security, and therewith in and ure the value of property a great meas- the credit 5000 | of the place ; but also the opinion of commonalty þÿ its faith in the establishments of justice (and along therewith in the whole public administration) but 4000 ; when, as often open transgressions remain unpunished, on account of there being seldom two witnesses to the act, and the guilty being aware, that a mere denial will do ; when the experience of the judge and his valuation of the circumstances, and thus often his sentence signifies nothing; when in the same cases, where vou pretend to have a prompt administration of justice, and recommend summary and verbal proceedings, opportunity is given for appeals without motives or object, by written proceedings and delays for as many weeks, as there often would be required minutes in other countries of English tongue, for a final settlement of the case, then the administration of justice, at least as far as it interests many, must fall short of

its purpose, if not worse; and neither the personal respectability of the officials nor high salaries will help that. The common people, also when in contact with public authorities, do only respect whatever has strength and gives results. Sentences which their own plain understanding overrules, or which are only given to be sentenced over again, and destroy punishments that no for one the cares their respect law and about, for the judge. It is by perfect publicity (even if that is to be paid for) which alone makes it practicable, that the judge should be allowed to decide cases on the general evidence ; and by the finality of the judgements (as the ordinary rule:) that law and justice can conquer good will and influence with this population; as long as nothing shall be done in this respect, but, with the exception of some insignificant publicity in common policecases, there is rather shown a tendency to formalise and increase writings; þÿ it is not considered expedient to recommend a permanent augmentation of the expenses of the islands for the administration of justice. These remarks are less applicable with regard to the administrative police, although the efficiency also of that must be weakened in consequence of the abovementioned defects þÿ f. ex. a single policeman has but little security in the execution of his duty. When the intended new laws against Vagrancy and other nuisances shall be put in force, if they are not to be as the former ones, all but dead letters, there will no doubt

be required somewhat larger means of action than these now at disposal, and certainly a different use of those means. It is also desirable, that the police- masters should not partly be obliged to look for other means of subsistence. Under the Government's proposition now before the Council, the policemasters in St. Croix, and St. Thomas are intended only to have to do with administrative matters and proceedings, including investigations in public cases, the judicial functions also in police suits to be referred to the ordinary judges. The Elcefion of the New Schoolmaster. Heinrich Eschokke in his work Das Gold- " macher-Porf," relates an amusing incident, the election of a new schoolmaster. " The old of schoolmaster, who was a dissipated character, being drowned, the parishioners were called together to elect a new one. The first of the parish authorities, Mr. Brentzel, opened the meeting by a speech. As the office of schoolmaster was vacant, and was one of the least important in the parish (for the salary was only forty gilders a-year, þÿ about $16 66), he was happy to be able to recommend to the parish a suitable man, willing to fill the place. This was the tailor, Mr. Specht, whose trade was very dull, and who was, moreover, related to him, the speaker, on the mother's side. The host of the Eagle came forward to propose, as an amendment, that þÿ his poor cousin Hchluck, a lame fiddler, should fill the office ; for he was willing to do it, considering the poverty of the parish, for a salary of only thirty-five gilders per annum. In weighing the qualification of the candidates, he hoped it would be remembered that Mr. Schluck had a large family. This, with the fact of the saving of five gilders, would doubtless influence the votes of the parishioners. Specht the tailor, as he saw that many of the voters were very much taken with this tempting offer, came forward to give the fiddler a very bad character, and, further, offered to perform all the duties of the office at a salary of only thirty gilders.

At this the fiddler was so enraged, that he called the tailor by many most disgraceful names, and again offered himself at a reduced salary. Twenty five gilders would be enough for him. The tailor, who could not go below this, declared he would call Schluck before the magistrate to answer for the libels he had uttered, and so gave up further competition. The voters were accordingly prepared to install the fiddler in the office of schoolmaster, when Oswald stood forward and spoke þÿ " What ! will you give more to your cow-herd, and even to your swine-herd, than to the man to whom you would confide the instruction of your children in piety and useful knowledge ? Are you not ashamed of such a sin ? I know your parish purse is empty ; and the poor people, who can hardly gain potatoes and salt, let alone bread, cannot afford to pay for schooling. I will make a third offer : I will bo your schoolmaster, and demand no salary ! It shall not cost the parish a farthing : only let mo have the place." The Goldenthalers looked at each other in amazement. Some objected to the proposal : they did not know what such a man would teach their children , perhaps the black art ! But the majority in the meeting considered chiefly the. saving of twenty-five gilders yearly , and cried out that Oswald should by all means be the schoolmaster. Accordingly, he was elected."

The report of the French Minister at Turin adds that it was suppressed, and that Turin and Piedmont were tranquil. A telegraphic despatch from Bellinzona of the 8th inst announces, however, that the gates of Milan were closed, and it was supposed that the insurrection which had been previously suppressed had re-commenced. Of course the Austrian accounts are scarcely to be credited, and the origin of the movement is at present involved in obscurity. One statement is, that the report of the death of the Emperor of the French had been circulated, and the official contradiction of it by tho authorities had so excited the public mind that the people had recourse to arms. The other story is, that the "affray" was got up as an excuse for the Austrians to remove their forces into Lombardy. A manifesto of Mazzini had been posted up in the streets, and the valiant Kossuth has turned up opportunely by publishing in Longarian nation, announcing that " in the name of don a well-written exciting address to the Hunhis nation he has made alliance with the Italian nation." He says the moment of insurrection is at hand ; and the whole tenor of the document looks as if some combined scheme between tho

Italians and the Hungarians had been preconcerted to destroy their oppressors, the Austrians Kossuth promises to be shortly amongst his people ; " Hungary after the victory the state property is to be divi- is to be his right wing, Italy his left ; ded amongst the army and the families of the victims of patriotism ; but the coward end the traitor shall die." The relations of Turkey and Austria were just assuming very hostile complications, when this movement in Lombardy threatens the most serious results. Whilst superficial politicians were discussing the dismemberment of Turkey as an affair which could be settled off hand in the most simple manner by the partition of the European provinces between Russia and Austria, this insurrection in Lombardy upsets all these theories, and brings the chances of warfare nearer to France. With the great armies under Jellachich now set in motion, we cannot but think this movement in Lombardy ill-timed ; and looking at the cause of liberty, and the fatal example of France, we dread the hostile operations of all parties. The spirit of mischief seems on foot, and with one despot in France, in western Europe, ready to make an unprovoked aggression upon any power to extend the limits of France, and another powerful despot at Warsaw, in eastern Europe, also ready to stretch the limits of Russia towards Constantinople ; we are sorry to say that " united" Germany furnishes no bulwark whatever against the designs of either power. We therefore repeat

the expression of our alarm, that the present complications threaten the peace of Europe. Effects of Drainage on the Temperature of the Soil. þÿ All the rain that falls upon our fields must either be carried away by natural or artificial drainage, or, having thoroughly saturated the soil on which it falls, be left upon the surface to be carried off by evaporation. Now, every gallon of water thus carried off by evaporation, requires as much heat as would raise five and a half gallons from the freezing to the boiling point ! Without going to extreme cases, the great effects thus lost upon vegetation cannot fail to be striking, and I have frequently found the soil of a field well drained, higher in temperature from

10 degs. to 15 degs. than that of another field which had not been drained, though in every other respect the soils were similar. I have observed tho effects of this on growing crops, and I have seen not only a much inferior crop on the undraincd field, but that crop harvestod fully throe weeks after the other, and owing to this circumstance and the setting in of unsettled weather. The division of the functions presently discharged by the policemasters alone is intended to enable those officers to altend effectually to the manifold administrative business, on the able performance of which the general security for person and property and in many respects the municipal interest depend ; to do away with all cause for prejudice against the impartiality of the policejudges in cases concerning the members of die police forces, and particularly respecting acts undertaken under general or special orders of the chief magistrate, above all, to ensure a real organisation of the police in each island, and therewith uniformity of action in the different jurisdictions. This can evidently be effected, as long as the organisation is new, only by an effective superintendence, and the Governor requires no new authority for if such pose ; it might be required, that pur- functions were to be performed by another functionary attached to the Governor on his own responsibility; under such an arrangement the guarantees, that eventual complaints against the police could meet redress, would be rather increased than otherwise. But against the plan proposed, it can be said, in salaries that the above proposed the first place for the services of gentlemen policemasters are too low well to secure the qualified ; that the conduct of the policemasters, and as a necessary condition, an exten-

sive knowledge both of things and persons, can not at all be supplied by the ever so careful superintendence of the Governor or his Assistant ; further that the relation between policemaster and police-judge will easily give rise to increase of writings and to references and postponements annoying to the public ; but the greatest objection seems to be this, that a policemaster by losing his authority as judge would no doubt in the present state of affairs lose a great part of the necessary authority, and if it should happen, as it may and almost can be foreseen, that the Judge in one or another jurisdiction entertained divergent views or was prejudiced against the police establishment, the consequences would be very serious. On these grounds it is considered advisable, that the policcmaster should remain policejudge (not however in cases of petty debts;) it is not supposed, that this circumstance needs to throw insurmountable obstacles in the way of an effective and uniform organisation and action of the whole police system. On this supposition it would be proper, that the salary for the policemaster ought to be fixed at $3000 in St. Thomas and at $'2500 in St. Croix, with $300 for travelling expenses to each. Besides there should be allowed full payment of the office-expenses, so as to secure the services on each place of at least one able and trustworthy head clerk or assistant, and with a view to have as much writing as possible expedited by the upper or lower police officers without in-

jury to the service. With respect to the close relations between many functions of the policemasters and the municipal interests, and as hitherto no official has been specially charged with the communal affairs (as Town-magistrate, Mayor) it may hereafter he thought proper, that at least some such duty be united to the office of policemaster, with indemnification, and eventually with some limitation of the judicial business. Reservation in this respect might be made in

issuing appointments to these offices ; also with respect to the officials in St. Thomas as far as regards such judicial business at St. Johns, as might be made over to them in the event of the judge'soffice being vacant which is however by no means considered advisable. The appointment of a police assistant at Kings Hill, þÿ should the present Police-jurisdiction of the centre district be done away with, þÿ does not appear decidedly necessary, as the functions may at less expense just as well be done by a head clerk or a police sergeant stationed there. But on the question relative to the appointment of police assistants as well as regarding the other officers of the exeeutive police and all the office expenses, it is not seen how any distinct proposals can be made, in as far as there is no precise statement before us as to the number and quality of officers required and their employment, þÿ generally no plan for the organisation of the police service. Whether the police force generally be regulated on the military principle of which is thought preferable, (it is however not necessary, that military be exclusively employed) and whether the mounted police soldiers mentioned in the motives should be at daily disposal in the jurisdictions for the general service of the police, þÿ say for citing and carrying messages this would be of great moment as to the expenses of the police administration ; it is believed, that by a proper employment of such a police force, the policemasters (and the budget)

would be relieved from the burdensome " horse hire for policemen," whereby either the policemaster or the service incurs loss. It is thought right, that the military furnishes to the police service such force as may be necessary, and can be spared, and otherwise be qualified for such service ; that it is desirable, that policemen be kept as far as possible under a formal discipline, and that they be strictly forbidden to traffic or to be in any private employment. New York Herald, February 16, 1853. The Plague in llic West Indies. IMPORTANT ADVICE TO SHIPMASTERS. to the editor of the herald. A malignant and fatal fever having prevailed as an epidemic throughout the West Indies, during

the past summer, and still continuing its ravages in many places, I consider it a part of my public duty to make known such remedies as have proved highly successful here, trusting that, through the extensive circulation of your journal, they may reach other infected districts, and, in some measure, alleviate the evil. I make no pretension whatever to medical knowledge, all my experience having been acquired at the sick bed, and from the perusal of such medical books as have fallen in my way. The emetic and purge I have found most beneficial in this fever, are those recommended in a work of Dr. W. Beach, of New York, on family medicine. As soon as the symptoms of the fever appear, such as headache, nausea, lassitude, pains in the limbs or back, d-c., a powerful emetic should be immediately administered, followed, as soon as practicable, by an active purge, soaking the feet frequently in hot mustard or ley water. If the relief be not speedy, and the blood tends to the head or bowels, causing internal heat or irritation, particularly in the latter, with coolness or unequal circulation in the extremities, there is danger of congestion, and recourse must be had at once to mustard poultices, commencing on the inside of the legs at both ancles, and removing them upwards, as the burning becomes insupportable, to the calves, the thighs, then to the wrists, middle and upper parts of the arms, and, should there be much pain in the head, to the temples, behind the ears, and on

the back of the neck, bathing the head frequently with diluted camphorated spirits or new rum ; and during these applications, acidulated mucilaginous drinks should be freely given, and cooling applications, wet cloths, Ac., applied to the bowels. Stronger mustard poultices should be repeated on the outside of the legs and arms, if all danger of congestion be not removed, and any symptoms of fever still remain. The patient should be again freely purged with a mixture of olive and castor oils, with the addition of a little lime juice. When the fever bvcaks, quinine or some other tonic may be given ; there is, however, little danger of remission. Bleeding may be necessary in extreme cases, and must be left to the discretion of the physician, although in most that have come under my notice, it has had no good effect. This fever seems to act like a poison, received from the atmosphere into the system, and should be expelled as such, from the stomach and intestines, before it has time to corrupt the blood, a few hours delay often proving fatal Those who fall victims to this disease, usually become putrid and discolored as soon as dead. By the above course of treatment, I have seen restored to health many patients who had already vomited black ; and in the first stages, the timely application of the emetic and purge has frequently effected a cure. This fever runs from three to five days, and is so treacherous as often scarcely to declare itself on the surface, and requires the utmost
vigilance and attention on the part of the nurse as well as the physician. John L. Wilson, United States Commercial Agent. Cape Haytien, January, 1853.

HTS MAJESTY the KING oil Ihc draft of the Kiidgct for the financial year 1853-34. (Concluded.) The allocations are considered too high, even allowing for the higher expenses of living in St. Thomas. We cannot think that there can he any great objection to the uniting of the dealingmaster's office to that of the judge's (especially if the latter office be not charged with the pol ice cases :) and a salary of $3200, inclusive of travelling expenses for public cases, we think sufficient; as regards the amount of the office expenses, no confutation can be made; it ought however not to exceed much more than $2000. With respect to the notary's office must be observed, that the emoluments stated, say about $1800 (fees) are very uncertain, and depend in a great measure upon exceedingly high charges, which cannot be sustained for any long period ; further that a great part of the notary's emoluments, according to the customs of the place, are derived from the drawing up of documents, translations and such business more properly belonging to lawyers and translators, and which a judge ought not to be allowed to undertake, which however can not, without inconvenience to the public, be separated from the notary's office; even the ordinary business of the notary such as the protesting of bills, attestations ot the identity or signature of persons, is not liked to be done by others than by the notary himself; but if the notary's functions should be united with those of the judge, that inconvenience would

often arise. It is therefore considered, that the notarial office in St. Thomas ought to remain an independent office, without salary or subvention from the State-treasury; the amount which on account thereof might be struck off the credit side of the budget 15 No. II, would scarcely be considerable, when the revision of the fees so much demanded takes place. Whilst thus the expenses proposed in the Budget for the lower court and police offices in St. Croix and St. Thomas, say $23304 and $8590 amount to $31954, the majority proposes the expense for the same to be $26212 and $13700, or $39912, as a normal disbursement it must however be observed, that a part of those expenses, as rated in the draft, would not necessarily be permanent, þÿ The amendment proposed, sub IN'o. 2, and on the other hand, that the calculated amounts of fees, which should go to the State-treasury, cannot be expected to yield anything like the amounts rated. The increase of this branch of expenditure with about $8000, according to the proposal of the majority has been proposed to be covered by the abolition of the office of the chief magistrate in St. Thomas, and that of the secretary's office attached thereto. The functions of this office (according to the draft to be called President and Vice Governor) are to be the same, and probably somewhat more extensive, that is to say with regard police to affairs, than those which are now administered by "the comman- dant" and " the Royal Council ;" when

the majority assumes that those functions are of no consequence and could without injury be referred to the decision of the Government in St. Croix, this cannot be assented to ; on the contrary it is firmly believed, that the want of a local chief magistrate (even if some appointment did not prove satisfactory) would be felt much in St. Thomas and give so much dissatisfaction, that you would soon have to institute that office anew, if even it were temporarily done away with.

£ t\ In that commercial place, which is often overstocked with foreigners and among them bad characters, with a country population not well regulated and with worse neighbours ; þÿ and where the only source of wealth, commerce, above all things requires security, it is not considered advisable to have only a policemaster, commander of the " fort," number of co-ordinate officials, judge, intendant of customs, harbourmaster þÿ stadshauptman, brandmajor; conflicts have not been unfrequent at least but a few years back. Some cases will always have to be referred to the superior Government in St. Croix, the more easily when a communication by steam could be secured 3 or 4 times a week (now you can only count on corresponding twice a week) þÿ but for the event of serious disturbances or attempts thereat, of large fires or the like misfortunes, which do not give long notice, the want of a resident chief magistrate, invested with the superior direction would give cause to serious apprehension. It is well known how unwilling the commanders of foreign men-of-war whose crews often give trouble, are to enter into communication with any subordinate civil authority. That the different offices are sometimes filled by " deputies" or by persons only acting p. t., can of course not be avoided. To refer foreigners with reclamations etc., to the Governor in St. Croix might sometimes not be practicable. In the country of St Thomas (and St. Johns) there are circumstances of such difficulty, so mi-

serable a decrease of prosperity with indications of a retrograding tendency, that there is plenty to do lor a chief magistrate of talent and of feeling; þÿ but without acknowledged authority and the personal influence which is a condition thereof, there is not much to be expected under such circumstances. Besides it is not alone the commonalty, but also the merchants and others domiciled, or travellers who find a protection, a satisfaction in knowing that there is somebody above the official with whom dispute or conflict occurs, to whom they can easily be applied without delay, and may be expense of forwarding complaints to another Island. The draft sub II. C. a., ought therefore not to be struck out ; þÿ in how far there possibly might be effected any reductions of expenditure about the secretary's office, on this item no opinion can be formed presently.

in the treasurer's salary in St. Croix can neither be recommended by the minority; it cannot be of any great interest to the present official, who has not petitioned without not warrant for it, and necessity regu- circumstances to do late as higher expenses for future times. The same minority cannot either coincide in the remarks of the majority, respecting the military commander in chief, as it is evidently in the interest of the Islands, that all the authority which can consistently be united in the hands of the Governor, shall be and ought to be seen to be there. That the Governor þÿ particularly when the senior officer receives some pay for matters of military command þÿ should charge himself with the detail of the service or demand references to him, more than he himself considers to be necessary, can certainly not be presumed ; but it must be expected that the questions concerning the regulation of that particular service, when they do present themselves, will be regulated by the administration concerned, can the minority accede to the proposal nor in regard of a new regulation of the Governor's allowance, notwithstanding the present figure is fixed at a low rate, as the Governor has not demanded any

increase thereof; nor should there be adopted the recommendation made, that the salary of the secretary to Government, now $3200 shall, on vacancy be fixed at $3000; difficult and responsible offices, as the abovementioned, for which but few can be expected to concur, cannot well be voted before-hand at $200 more or less. The minority can neither enter upon the proposal made, now to fix reduced salaries for the judges of the Uppercourt, in the case of vacancy; those qualifications, which should be required from a Judge of Appeals, say professional eminence and a full perception of what /if may be the distinguishing: " p features of the place and the people, cannot be secured for $2500 a year. By appointing a number of superior Judges on smaller salaries, you weaken the responsibility of an office so important and so honorable, and the number will not compensate for other defects. That the total amount of the draft II. B. b, and c., and II. C. b, and c., together amounting to $31954 be appropriated to the expenditure for lower courts and police administrations in the islands St. Croix and St. Thomas. With reference to what has been stated in the foregoing by the minority respecting the subordinate judicial- and police-establishments, and especially what it has advanced with regard to the business attached to the different offices, and the salaries for certain offices, also in regard of the inexpediency in this present matter to establish definite conclu-

sions relative to the subordinate police and its officials, its organisation and the salaries for the same, the minority must be of the opinion, that the only subjects on which the Colonial Council had to pass their opinion were, the items in the draft sub II. Wilmer and Smith's European Times, March 1, 1853. The Women of England and America.

In the papers brought by the British and North American Mail Steam-ship Europa, we find a lengthy letter, purporting to be from the pen of Julia Gardner Tyler, wife of ex-president Tyler addressed to the Duchess of Sutherland and others, in answer to the appeal from the women of England with regard to the American Slave-laws, which appears in the Richmond Enquirer, January 28. It commences by stating that the women ol the United States, with hut few exceptions, confine themselves within that sphere for which God seemed to have designed them, and that it was utterly impossible to expect that they would assemble in person or by proxy for the purpose of framing an answer ti> It continues : þÿ the address of the women of England. " Nay, I must, moreover, in all frankness, declare to you, that the women of the South, especially, have not received your address in the kindest spirit. They see, or fancy they see, in the fact that the address which you have made them was handed to you. already prepared for signature, by the editors oft he newspaper press of England, and that, according to the admission of the Duchess of Sutherland in her opening address to your convention, your convention itself is hut the offspring of the same political newspaper press ; I say, they sec enough in all this to excite, not their sympathies, hut their apprehensions. They see, or fancy that they sec, in your movement, the lingers of your greatest statesmen. The Countess of Dervy, the Viscountess Palmcrston, the

Countess of Carlisle, Lady John Russcl, not to mention others of distinction ami notoriety, would scarcely be complimented by a supposition that they had signed or openly approved such an address without the concurrence of their husbands. The women of the United States comprehend the fact that all confederacies have heretofore, in the history of the world, been broken up and destroyed by the machinations of foreign governments. If the Achninn and other leagues could not withstand the machinations of the powers of their day, how truly sensitive ought we to he on a point which proved so fatal to them. We know that there is hut one subject on which there is the possibility of wrecking the hark of this Union, a possibility, however, which I trust is very remote, and to that very subject you have given your attention. Nor is this suspicion in any degree removed b v the fact on which you predicate your address; namely, the fact that your country inflicted on her then colonies the curse of slavery in opposition to their frequent and solemn protests. Vou are altogether correct in ascribing whatever Ihere is of immorality or crime, in the present condition of the Southern States, to your own England. The great slave-market, in which England has enjoyed a monopoly, was thus lost to her ; and, from that moment she began to discover that there was something rather immoral in the traffic. # Your tears arc made to flow freely over the sad and melancholy privations of the children of Africa, to whom the bread of

life is represented as denied. Your assertion could only have been derived from some dealer in, and retailer of, fiction. The crocodile, good sisters of England, is said to cry most piteously ; hut woe to the unhappy traveller who is beguiled by its tears. # It is better for both you and us that we abstain, in future, from all possible interference

with each other in the domestic concerns of our respective countries. In the first place, such interference comes with ill grace from either of us, and can be received with no favor. In morals we believe ourselves quite your equals, and therefore it sounds harshly in our ears to be admonished by you of our sins, real or imaginary. Each of us will find abundant employment in the performance of our respective duties. If you wish a suggestion as to the suitable occupation of your idle hours, I will point you to the true field for your philanthropy, the unsupplied wants of your own people of England. In view to excite your most active sympathies I remember to have seen lately that there were in the city of London alone 100,000 persons who rose in the morning without knowing where or how they were to obtain their 'daily bread.' Go, my good Duchess of Sutherland, on an embassy of mercy to the poor, the stricken, the hungry, and the naked of your own land, cast in their laps the superflux of your enormous wealth ; a single jewel from your hair, a single gem from your dress, would relieve many a poor female of and destitute. England who is now # cold, # Leave it to the and shivering, women of the South to alleviate the sufferings of their dependants, while you take care of your own : the negro of the South lives sumptuously in comparison with the 100,000 of the white population of London." After observing that the ladies of England have no occasion to leave their shores for illustrations more

heart-rending than can be found in the Slave States, of the cruelty of separating husbands and wives, fathers and children, by the proceedings of the Admiralty, as exemplified in the system of press-gangs, the letter continues: þÿ "We prefer to follow our own conception of what it is proper for us to do. Our eyes are turned across the ocean, not in the direction of England, but to Africa. The footprints of our policy arc seen in the colonies there established, already become independent states, in the voluntary emancipation of slaves by our citizens as preparatory of emigration to Africa, a course of emancipation which, from 1790 to 1850, has increased our table in Virginia of free Negroes in the ratio of 301 pe r cent., while the white population has only increased 102£ per cent., and the slaves but G4jf percent. These interesting statistics 1 extract from a memorial recently presented to the Legislature of Virginia, asking additional aid to further the colonization of free Negroes in Liberia. Thus we seek to retribute the wrongs done by England to Africa, by returning civilization for barbarism, Christianity for idolatry. # America might love England if England would permit her. A common descent, a common language, mutual interests, and, to a great extent, a common heritage of freedom, should draw the two nations together. The disposition of the Southern mind (I speak what I do know) is to cultivate the closest friendship with England. Nearly all of the Southern people

are the descendants of the first settlers. They have kindred blood almost unmixed by emigration, flowing in their veins. But, if England will sever these ties ; if, instead of cultivating good feeling with us, she chooses rather to subject us to taunt, to ridicule, to insult in its grossest form ; and, above all, improperly to interfere in our domestic affairs; it she scatters her nobility among us, first to share our hospitality, and then to abuse us ; if, what is still worse, she sends her emissaries, in the persons of members of Parliament, to stir up our people to mutiny and revolt; if, which is quite as objectionable, her public press shall incite her women, and the more

a ir Air it & illustrious for birth the worse it makes the matter, to address us homilies on justice, humanity, and philanthropy, as if we had not, like themselves, the advantage of civilization, and the lights of Christianity, with all the desire to cultivate relations of undying amity, the men of the United States, deriving their spirits from their mothers and their wives, may be forced into the adoption of a very different feeling with regard to Great Britain." The letter is signed "Julia Gardner Tyler," and is dated "Sherwood Forest, Virginia, Jan. 2-1, 1853."

The mode of argument known as tu qcoque is as universal as human passion. It is that where a charge is replied to by a counter þÿcharge an imputation by a counter imputation. It is common in all countries, and among all grades of society : but it is usually held by philosophers to pertain more exclusively to the half-educated. Women and children mostly employ it, perhaps without knowing its logical significance or rather insignificance: and the ignorant and the ill-bred know no other formula in the science of reasoning. " You're a bad 'un," says an indignant costermonger to a peccant peripatetic successor of Tubal Cain þÿ a travelling tinker. " You're another," is the replication. This is the mode of argument designated by logicians, from Aristotle down to Archbishop VVhatley and Mr. Mill, tu quoque. The replication of the American ladies, interested in negro slavery, to the ladies of England who signed or sanctioned the address confected some month or so since at Stafford House upon this subject, as made "through the organ of Mrs. Tyler," the wife of an ex-President of the United States, is a pregnant example of tu quoque. The address sent forth from Stafford House was short, if not sweet; it was certainly courteous ; it did not blame America alone, but nssumed part of the blame to England, and it ended in the moderate intrcaty that the women of the United States would use their influence to obtain for the poor slaves, 1st. The rights of marriage, so that husband,

wife, and children should no longer be liable to bo torn asunder at the will of the " owner and, 2d, Access to education, so that it should no longer be criminal to teach slaves to read. Moderate and reasonable they were, and women calling themselves Christians ought naturally to rejoice to bo so besought, as well as eagerly resolve to do all that as women they might properly do to lessen, if they could not terminate, the horrors of slavery ; but what is the actual fact ? To this address there have been no fewer than three sharp replies, two of which, as being anonymous, inay be dismissed from present consideration þÿ the last being signed in the name of the wife of the ex-President Tyler; and in this, as well as in each of the others, while the main question is wholly avoided, objurgatory vituperation, some of it well founded, though all of it illogical and unreasonable, as well as in the worst taste, is employed to an extent almost incredible. Slavery, if defensible, should bo defended by argument and not by objurgation ; but it is on objurgation alone that Mrs. Tyler rests her case þÿ not, be it said in passing, so much in favour of that bondage which is the blot on the free institutions of the United States, as against the institutions, or perhaps more strictly speaking, as against the forms of society that exist in this country. The Stafford House address grounds its appeal on the law of nations, as well as on the doctrines of Christianity. Mrs. Tyler replies, not

that slavery docs not exist in the United States, not that the slave is not ill-treated and despised, not that it is a damning fact which stands as a national stigma, to be effaced at the earliest opportunity from the national conscience ; but that there are hundreds of thousands of paupers in England, that the rich are every day growing richer, and the poor poorer, that the aristocratic portion of the community have no " bowels of compassion" for their fellow-subjects, that Ireland is a wretched, oppressed, God-abandoned country, and a number of other allegations of the same nature. The subject of negro slavery is but incidentally touched upon by her llucnt pen; ami then,

only to put it in a light new at least to this country. The slaves, she says, are well fed and well þÿclothed nay they are even petted by tlie wives of their owners þÿ as idle women will pet a pony or sometimes a pig þÿ therefore she concludes they are happy. This, however, is a non sequitub which cannot be allowed in any form. When Mrs. Tyler has learned to reason as well as to objurgate, she will see the futility as well as the folly of such a mode of argument in such a grave matter. Granted that the pauperism of England is a reproach to the immense wealth of England ; granted that the poor and the lowly are outraged and despised by the rich and the powerful in this country ; granted that Ireland has been down-trodden for seven centuries, until political oppression has emasculated the national mind, and social suffering has destroyed the national virility of the race which vegetates upon its soil ; þÿ granted all these things (and it is freely conceded to Mrs. Tyler that they are undeniable), does it offer a single excuse, to say nothing of even the slightest shadow of justification, for negro slavery in the United States of America ? Two negatives, in morals at least, do not make an affirmative ; nor will objurgation of the oppressions and wrongs of other nations purify the American character from the foul taint cast upon it by negro slavery. And even though Mrs. Tyler makes her imaginary slave a being so happy that bondage would seem, according to her, to be the normal condition of existence which men of

all colours should strive to attain, she will be none the worse for recollecting that Christianity has always propounded the very reverse of Burke's atrocious maxim, that " vice loses half its deformity by losingall its grossness." This is what Mrs. Tyler tells of the negro slave in the United States : these are her references from the premises she puts forward. Glancing over the facts, not denying them, but treating them very lightly, she says the negroes have liberty to attend chapel ; but is that a valid reason why it should be a breach of the law to teach them to read ? The separation of husband and wife, she avers, is " a thing of rare occurrence." " Often" and " seldom" are, however, relative terms, and convey no distinct or accurate idea. If, however, the atrocity occurs but seldom, why not give it up altogether? Truth admits no middle term. Mrs Tyler affects to assume that the Stafford House Address is a political movement, originating either with English statesmen or English newspapers ; and that its concealed object is to break up the Union. This might have been a feasible supposition had tho address proposed war against slavery ; but not a word of the kind was contained in that document. It left, in fact, slavery itself untouched; it spoke only of certain rights of humanity ; it asked for no agitation, no political effort ; it appealed merely to the natural feelings of woman's heart, and intreated of the women of America that they would employ, silently and unobtrusively,

that infiuence which they could not but possess, to help forward the amelioration of the condition of the poor negroes. In sober seriousness the whole reply þÿ pedagogic and irrelevant as it þÿis is a grotesque exhibition of a very mournful conclusion. Slaveholders become, tfter a time, incapable of perceiving or appreciating truth and justice ; and the vituperative accusations of Mrs. Tyler and her friends þÿ paupers .' Look at your press-gangs ? " Look at your Look at Ireland !" only prove that a long course of violent denegation of the dictates of conscience at last deprives even the wcll-educatod mind of the power of discriminating between right and wrong. History has recorded, and every day's experience of life attests its truth, that one of the most evident, most natural, and most lamentable results of a system which does violence to the voice ol conscience, and outrages tho feelings of human nature, is that the offender, whether a nation or an individual, after persevering for a while in crime, becomes morally blind, deaf, and irrational. To this point of abnormal degradation has negro slavery reduced the southern states of tho North American Republic ; and Mrs. Tyler may as well try to make black white as attempt to prove the contrary of such a sell evident proposition.

St. Thomas Times , March 19. The R. M. S. Trent, Captain Bevis, from Chagres, &c., arrived here on Thursday night. General Santa Ana. (Mexican General), family, and suite, came passengers by her, en route to Vera Cruz. We have been obligingly favored by passenger a with the following interesting manuscript: þÿ The Route across Nicaragua.

We arrived at San Juan del Sur the Pacific þÿ terminus of this route þÿ on the 27th of February, after a fine passage of 12 days from San Francisco, in the steam-ship Brother Jonathan, Captain Baldwin, U. S. Navy, of the Vanderbilt Nicaragua line. San Juan del Sur which owes its þÿ notoriety to this Company þÿ is a very small settlement, with a tolerably safe bay, and not above half a dozen houses, the best building among them being the Company's Agency. Our mules being in readiness, we did not remain there longer than was necessary to procure our transit tickets, and settle for the transportation of our luggage, for which we are charged fifteen cents a pound ; and after receiving our cheques, we started on our land journey, of 12 miles to Virgin Bay, which we reached the same evening. The road over which we travelled is almost level, and remarkably smooth, but notwithstanding its present good condition, the Company, by very judicious improvements, such as cutting ditches, and building strong bridges, seems to take every precaution for the safety and convenience of passengers during the approaching wet season. Navy Bay situated at the head of the lake þÿ þÿ is a miserable little town, built of straw huts and canvas tents, <J-c., peopled by ragged and filthy natives, who exhibit more regard for the dimes than the civilisation of their foreign guests. Five hundred and fifty passengers are not easily accommodated in such a place notwithstanding : the " bunks" two and three tiers high, (for the prive-

lege of sleeping wherein, besides the payment of a dollar, one is made to feel that he receives a great obligation), the American canvas hotels," " and native-bamboo " boarding houses" were soon filled, and we, among many, roamed about till a late hour, in search of a spot whereon to stretch our mule-jostled bodies. After long wandering between an open field, and the dirty floor of the " United States," where we took our supper, we gave the preference to the latter, being as less exposed ; and surrounded by ladies and children, soon fell asleep. Company's Agents, Although our luggage who continue supply in the charge " ways of and the means" for their transportation until delivered on board the steamers at Grey Town ; the Company's responsibility ceases at Virgin Bay, where we return our cheques, and become the guardians of our own property for the rest of the journey. The luggage mules not having all arrived during the night, it was late the next morning before our trunks and oarpet-bags could be recovered and shipped on board the lake steamer, so that we had ample time to stroll about in quest of fruit, and to admire the beautiful lake, with its lofty " Ometepe," and other Islands, which lay several miles from shore. The Company's steamers on the lake are the Ometepe and Central America, the former named after an island-mountain on the the lake, said to be about 6,000 feet high. The Central America being laid up, we were all tightly packed on board the Ometepe, and sent down the

lake, to fort San Carlos, where we arrived at day break the next morning, Tuesday, the 1st instant. There was, it seemed to me, a great deal of unnecessary delay at Virgin Bay, from which point we had been informed we would leave at noon on Monday, whereas it was 7 o'olock in the evening when we got under weigh. But, as you will percoivc from the sequel, notwithstanding the facility of the route (which undoubtedly superior is to that of Panama

ir . <o a d it a: ati without the railroad), and the civil, obliging Agents at the different points, the Company's arrangements are as yet very incomplete, and delay must, therefore, continue to occur, until a better system is established. This can only be effected by the addition of steamers on the lake and river, as whenever it happens that passengers arrive at one side while the steamers are at the other, they are bound to wait, and to submit to the most exorbitant charges for the worst possible accommodation and fare. From Fort San Carlos, situated at the junction same boat until reaching Toro," about 30 miles of the river with the lake, we continued in the " below, where the little steamer Director took us off in two trips, over the rapids, to Castillo, some 12 miles distant. At this place which þÿ takes its name from an old fort or castle, now in ruins þÿ the river steamers ought to have been in readiness to take us to Grey Town, but to our disappointment none of them had yet reached, so that again we had to submit to delay and expense, and, but for the kindness of the Agent, who allowed us to sleep in the Company's building, we should, like many others, have passed the night under heaven and our over-coats, all the bunks and available space in the few miserable public houses in the place having been filled by the passengers that came down in the first trip of the Director. The river being low, and the steamers still missing the next morning, the Agent agreed to the wish of some of the passengers to be sent

down in "bongos" (dug-outs), and open boats, partly at their own expense, and after a rainy journey of from 20 to 30 hours we reached Grey Town before the return of any of the steamers, which we met on our way with the passengers of the Daniel Webster and Prometheus , from New York and New Orleans. The scenery on the river is magnificent þÿ on either side the most luxuriant vegetation þÿ here, a green little island dividing the stream into two channels þÿ yonder, an alligator basking in the bright warm sun, or tho wreck of an old steamer on the bank, with its sides perforated by worms þÿ all lend a romantic wildncss to the scenery, on which the eye feasts with delight. But to this feeling succeeds one of astonishment at the primitive state of every thing around you. Nearly four centuries have rolled over the discovery and settlement of this Continent, and yet how little has this portion of it advanced from its primitive state! His home a hut built of bamboo and straw þÿ his food what grows spontaneously from the rich soil, or is raised with the least trouble, þÿ in ignorance, filth, indolence, and nakedness ; the half-civilized peasantry of Central America live on without the least knowledge of their importance, or any idea of their rights. There, as in almost all the other Spanish-American commonwealths, the ignorance of the masses, who can neither read nor write, places them entirely in the power of every ambitious demagogue, who finds it easy to be the tyrant of a people without the least knowledge of

its sovereign-rights. But it is to be hoped that civilization, will soon cease to blush for these countries, and that those at least through which day, themselves become " sister-stars" in the are the high-ways to the Golden State, will, one constellation. Then, under the influence of wise and liberal institutions, and by the example of our enlightened and enterprising people, their brilliant destiny will dawn. Grey Town þÿ the Atlantic terminus of our route þÿ is a small settlement, with a commodious harbor, where, according to the inhabitants, the wind blows and the rain falls every day in the year. Its population, now considerably thinned, does not exceed a few hundred inhabitants, composed of natives, Mosquito Indians, and foreigners ; of which latter nearly all are Americans, It is a sort of " Sovereign City," governed by a Municipal Council, legislative and executive, which acknowledges superior authority no to its

own. It has a Marshal and one Policeman, who watch over the peace of the town, and collect dues from canoes arriving from the interior þÿ added to which, there are a few muskets, and a diers. couple of cannon in the station-house, but no sol- Contrary to the custom in most " modern cities," gambling is strictly prohibited, and vagrants are shipped off to more congenial climes. I found a great deal of ill-feeling prevailing between the citizens and the Vanderbilt Company, arising, as far as I was able to ascertain, from the old sore of the Prometheus. The Company's ships no longer land their passengers, who are now immediately transferred to the river boats, by which means the trade of the town is seriously injured. The citizens, to retaliate, threaten to destroy the Company's buildings on the opposite side of the harbor, where, they assert, an illegal monopoly is carried on. Captain Churchill, of the Prometheus while I was there, refused passage to New York to several of the citizens, who proceeded in the British steamer to Aspinwall, hoping to meet the Pacific Mail Company's boat One great mischief arises from this quarrel, and that is, that the river steamers which ought to be waiting in the interior for passengers from California, are detained on this side to take off Atlantic passengers immediately on their arrival, in order to prevent the necessity of their being landed in Grey Town. >&<< þÿ þÿ

We give insertion to the following papers, which will explain themselves, and which were intended to have appeared in the pamphlet we purpoged publishing, regarding the proceedings of the first Colonial Council ; but being obliged, we regret to say, to relinquish our intentions in this respect, for reasons before stated in this Gazette, and considering the question treated of in these papers to involve important consider itions for a large class of this community, we deem it our duty to lay them before the public, in order that a grievance which has so long existed, has been so much complained of, and so often remonstrated against, should be more fully known and understood by those whose interests it affects. We consider any comment of ours unnecessary, but we beg leave to remark in reference to the superior privileges complained þÿof houses abroad, shall he obliged, in St. Croix, to and of whicli the subjoined extract from a Roval Rescript, dated 4th November 1787, will give some idea þÿ that, if there existed anything- in the condition or circumstances of the population of this colony in those days to render such extraordinary privileges, as were then granted to transient traders, necessary ; no sucli necessity now exists ; but on the contrary their continuance is felt by a large portion of our resident population as a sore injury, and it is to be hoped þÿ notwithstanding that the petition of our merchants and traders brought forward at the late Session of the Colonial Council, did not have that weight and influ-

ence to which it was considered to be entitled þÿ that whenever the highly important, and we may add, urgent question, is brought before the Colonial Council the colonies and the mother country, this " vexed for the adjustment or revision of the relations between question" will be finally set at rest in a manner that will fairly and equitably meet the just and reasonable expectations of the trading population of this Island.

Extract of Rescript of 4 th Nov. 1787, 8. " That the Danish Captains coming to tlie said Islands must, as well in their own as also in behalf of their ships' owners, sue their debtors by the more summary form of law-suit laid down for strangers and non-rcsidcnts, and must make use of the same not only as long as they are stationed in the said harbours, hut also when they, at a second or third voyage, intend to enforce older claims arising from credit given at former voyages ; aud, moreover, that such captains are to sell the goods they import not only from the vessels themselves, or in houses and stores which they rent or establish in the towns for such purpose, but may also sell them by their people, or hired negroes , who cu rry them, for sale through the country ; and lastly, that they, previous to their departure, may dispose of the remainder by public auction."

Copy of the Petition of the Merchants and Traders. To the Honorable the Colonial Assembly. May it please your Honorable Assembly. We the undersigned merchants and retail dealers in St. Croix, respectfully beg leave to state that we view with disappointment aud regret, the want of sufficient, just, and necessary protection to the resident traders of this island, as contained in the Draft of an ordinance at present before your honorable Assembly, purporting to " Regulate Trades and Professions in the Danish West India Possessions." The retailing of manufactured goods and other commodities, is a branch of business upon which the resident trading population of this island mainly depend for a subsistence. They arc in general owners of fixed property, they pay taxes, are liable to bear their share of all burdens necessary for the support of Government þÿ their interest is hound up with the prosperity or adversity of the colony : and being permanently resident, the fruits of their industry contribute to support the (now vastly increasing) poor of this island, and if successful in trade, their wealth, or means, adds to the general stability and welfare of the community of which they form a part. Contrast this with the facts as regards a transient trader, who can with superior privilges to the resident þÿ according to the provisions of this Draft þÿ come here and open a store for the retail of his goods, to the injury and prejudice of the established merchant or retailer, who, for the reasons before stated, is

unable to compete with liiin. A few months, or perhaps weeks, suffice in general to enable hiio to close up his business, and he departs elsewhere, withdrawing the entire nett proceeds of his goods þÿ capital and profits þÿ without those deductions

which naturally flow from the gains of those wh form integral parts of a community. Amendment proposed in the discussion which took place in the Colonial Council , on the Report of theCommittee on Trades and Professions being read. That all Masters of vessels, transient Traders, Supercargoes, or transient Agents of mercantile

consign their goods, wares, or merchandize, to a resident merchant, regularly established as such, and able to carry on business in his own name ; but in case such a transient person may wish to transact his own business while in the island, and be allowed the privilege of retailing out his goods, then he shall be obliged to obtain a burgher's brief to entitle him to sell by wholesale and retail according to 4 of this ordinance, and besides pay a transient duty of two and a half per cent to the Land Treasury, which shall he calculated upon the custom house valuation (according to the existing tariff) on the amount of goods 4-c. entered at same. No person shall be entitled to claim exemption from the stipulations contained in the .foregoing paragraph until after he shall have resided two years in this island. And any person who shall leave the island before the expiration of said time, and remain away over six months, unless his usual business shall have been in the mean time continued by an attorney, he shall on his return to the island be considered as having been non resident.

Remarks made in support of the foregt ing Petition ami Amendment, by the oth member. There is always much difficulty to In encountered in legislation when combating long existing grievances which press unjustly and sorely only upon one class of the community, particularly too when such grievances are maintained from long habit upon fallacious ideas of their being beneficial to the rest ; ideas which, as regards the present question, no more can be supported by sound reasoning than they can he upon principles of equity and sound policy. But it would he detaining the House too long, were 1 competent, to go into a detailed argument on these premises; I shall therefore content myself at present by alluding only to a few points connected with the petition of the merchants and traders of this island before this honorable Council, and in support of the amendment founded upon the same, which I have the honor to submit, leaving it to the good sense and justice of this assembly to mark by their votes, their disbelieve, approbation of a system will attempt to defend which few I þÿ a system, which, whatever may have been the animus of its origin, no just grounds I think can be shown to exist for desiring its longer continuance. The able remarks made on this subject by the honorable 2nd member for Christiansted who preceded me, has relieved me from saying much that 1 of intended to press upon the attention the Council regarding the grievance complained of by the petitioners; hut before proceeding

further, and in order to shew that this grievance is not an imaginary one, but so striking as to have attracted the notice, and called forth the remarks of disinterested and impartial observers, I must beg the indulgence of the Council to allow me to read a few passages bearing upon this subject, from a well

written pamphlet, published some years Ago, entitled "Denmark and St. Croix," which will be found more forcible and more appropriate than any remarks I am capable of making. In reference to this pernicious system, and unnatural treatment of the resident merchants, the writer remarks, " instead of endeavouring like all other states, to encourage the establishment of a flourishing trade in the Colonies, to enable the resident merchants agreeably to more correct ideas of trade, to conduct the commerce between the grower and the mother country, whereby the planters would not only gain time for exclusive employment in their pursuits, and immediately be placed in funds on the exchange of their products, but also be relieved from officiating as merchants in addition to ; their occupation as planters, and retaining agents and commissioners in a distant part of the world, unlike all other states, which hv this means, had erected in the colonies themselves flourishing towns ; &.c Denmark endeavoured to prevent local mercantile establishments at St. Croix in order that those advantages also might accrue, undivided to the mother country. This was effected by granting privileges to the Danish Captains trading to the island, to an extent that may be considered a phenomenon, per se, as regards the island, as well as general commercial history. This state of things, however, was very soon confirmed by laws and privileges, without any regard to the rising commercial body in the colo-

ny, who in lieu of being shown protection and encouragement, to render such privileges unnecessary, were on this very account, so oppressed, that they could not contend against them nor overcome them. The privileges which even at the present day, are exercised to their full extent by the Flcnsburg and Copenhagen Captains, consist in the right of selling by retail as well as by wholesale, both from on board the vessel and in stores on shore : on paying in the latter instance a trifling tax into the Land Treasury. It follows of course, that no merchant can compete with those who import their goods, sell them in the smallest quantities called for, on whom are not imposed any real or personal burthens." Here I might stop, fori think enough has been shown in what has been already said, and in what is stated in the body of the petition itself, to prove the existence of a grievance which oppresses the mercantile interests of this colony, and deprives us of a branch of trade which legitimately ought to be in the hands of the resident traders, but I cannot refrain from quoting one more observation which the writer makes in another place, and which will be found both natural and forcible ; it runs thus : " Denmark has privileges for her merchants, she prohibits masters of merchantmen keeping stores ashore to retail their cargoes and despoil the growers by forcing them on the latter as their sole merchants ; why does she uphold this impropriety in her colonies? These questions the colonists may well

ask, and even then the theme is not ex- Ivausted." It is a bad rule, Sir, according to a common adage, that dont work both ways þÿ but think ye, would a merchant, or a Captain, of this island be allowed to import a cargo of the produce of this country into Copenhagen or Flensburg, and open a store for the purpose of retailing out rum and sugar in the smallest quantities that might he called for? INo, I am quite sure he would not; he would soon find that there were barriers in his way, and that he was infringing the rightsofothers which mustnot he vio-

s v <o ife <© ir s: ATis, lated ; yet this is the very system against which we complain, and which continues to be exercised here to our injury, and which it is the object of the petition just read to have done away in common justice to the resident traders of this island. The majority of the committee on the draft of law now before the honorable Council, in their report have passed over this part of the subject rather lightly, and without that attention which, in my opinion its nature, and importance to a large class of this community, demands ; they, however, do not deny the existence of the grievance complained of. but on the contrary admit it, without however urging or pointing out a remedy. In the discussions however which took place in committee on this subject, the reasons assigned why it was considered inexpedient, and even dangerous, to take any steps towards remedying the evil at this juncture, was, that, it might have a bad influence on the minds of the members of the " Rigsdag" in deciding the question of compensation now before that Assembly. But I cannot admit this idea ; I should consider that such an argument would bean impeachment of their justice and common sense, for, what connexion is there between these two subjects? I must confess that I can see none ; nor can I suppose for one moment, that any Assembly of rational and honest men could be found at this day who would make the performance of an act of common justice towards one class of persons, contingent upon the perpetuation

ofthe undeniable grievances under which another class labors. In the first discussion that took place on this bill, His F.xcellency the Governor remarked, that, in framing the new draft of law, Government had left untouched the old regulations with regard to transient traders, as well as those privileges which had hitherto been granted to Danish Captains þÿ a course which 1 cannot hut regret, and which, with due deference, must say, in my opinion, would " be I more honored in the breach than the observance." IMor can I agree in opinion with His Excellency, in the value he sets on these privileges, as being in accordance with the national hospitality of Denmark towards strangers, or in the estimate he forms of the antiquity of the law on which they are founded. admire it þÿ Hospitality either is a beautiful trait; and I in the character of a nation or an individual, but I would take the liberty to remark, that there may be laws which age does not render venerable, and even hospitality ceases to be a virtue when exercised to the injury of the natural rights of others. No matter how these privileges may be viewed from prejudice or long custom; no matter how they may be regarded by those whose interest is unaffected by them, they are an undeniable grievance to the resident trader, against which he has a full right to remonstrate; they are opposed to those advantages which naturally should be secured to him as a resident of the island, upon whom rests the burthens of Government and whose

interests are involved in the prosperity or adversity of the colony þÿ without these undue privileges, granted to the non-resident traders and captains of vessels from the mother country, their legitimate advantagesas such are fully secured to them against foreign competition, þÿ for instance, in all goods the growth or manufacture ofthe mother country being exempt from duty, and all foreign goods imported in Danish bottoms from the mother country being subject to pay only half duties, with many others which it would be superfluous to mention. Why then cannot the trade on shore be

left in the hands of the resident merchants to whom it properly belongs? The whole tenor of the new drafts or regulations maintain the principle or of protection to each the profession, except respective trade mercantile ; for, what after all is a Store Tax or a Burgherbrief to a non-resident trader who desires to obtain the privilege of retailing out a valuable cargo of goods ? A mere þÿnothing it may, to be sure, add a little to the revenues ofthe Land Treasury, but considered as a protection to the resident trader it is but mockery and delusion. The non-resident planter is heavily taxed, why then hold out advantages to non-resident traders over those who remain in the colony and enrich it by their means and industry ? Oh, we are told if this was not done there would not he sufficient competition and the public would have to pay too high for the necessary articles of consumption. But those persons who would use such an argument can know little of the laws which regulate and govern, supply and demand in mercantile affairs, þÿ still less can they be observant of the over competition which exists around them not this town in articles of commerce in supplied either from Copenhagen or Flensburg; why then, may I ask, would it be different with the goods obtained from these places if a more correct policy was observed by throwing the trade with the mother country more into the hands of the resident merchants and leaving the captains in their proper þÿplace on board their ships ? But I may

be asked why was it that in by-gone times tiiere existed an opulent and an independent class of merchants here despite of this acknowledged cancer in the commercial policy of this island þÿ simply because other lucrative branches of trade then existed, which by the ever J changing circumstances which lime produces in the affairs of the world, have passed away. There was an extensive intercolonial trade with other islands, a lucrative trade with the Spanish Maine, and an important flourishing trade with the United þÿStates but these have long since passed away, and what have we ! left? Where are the opulent mcrchants we have heard of? These questions I need not answer. But, perhaps, by some strange perversion of ideas, an dent traders independent or or prosperous merchants are not con- class of resisidered advantageous or useful in this community, and that the colony would be better" without them ; it may be thought also more to the interest of the island to encourage in their place transient persons who will remain a few months of the year only to sell out their goods and then depart to enrich another community by their gains. If such be the object or desire, and that you are wishful of preventing the growth of a prosperous resident commercial class in this colony, you certainly cannot adopt a more effectual course than by continuing the existing regulations. I do not anticipate that you will adopt this amendment on the present occasion, but I shall not on that account cease to

agitate the question whilst I have the honor of a seat in this Council : it is a measure founded upon the broad basis of right, as wrell as upon those principles of correct policy which should govern the relations between the mother country and this colony. By bringing the question before the public, false prejudices I trust will give way before truth and reason, and people will eventually think correctly on the subject, notwithstanding it has been asserted that, policy, not truth, governs the world. þÿ " One Woman ! she requires no þÿeulogy of the toast drank at a recent celebration, was she speaks for herself."

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis ! Dear Sir ! I understand that a new system of' taxation is in view, and hope that it will be based on juster principles than the present, which I believe have no regard to the situation of the properties on which the taxes are charged, whether they are more or less profitable to the owners 4"c- Of course no definite steps will be taken before the Colonial Council has been heard, but in the mean time I think it the duty of those capable, to publish such items and elucidations, as may contribute to the just taxation above alluded to ; and thus give an opportunity that the subject may be thoroughly discussed in time. Your obedient servant, 31st March 1853. #

IVilmer and Smith's European Times, March 1, 1853. American Slavery. to the editor. Sir, þÿ I am grieved, though not surprised, to observe the spirit in which the address of the English ladies on the subject of slavery lias been received by their American sisters. As the address, however, modest and benevolent though it was, has not been universally approved here, so it may be hoped that the reply (or rather replies) will not be unanimously defended in America. It was perhaps wrong to expect the language of remonstrance, however gentle, to be received in the true and genuine Christian spirit which is rarely exhibited in such cases. It is not my purpose, however, either to defend the one or find fault with the other, as there is certainly much that requires reforming in both countries. But I wish to offer a few hints as to the way in which a beginning might, T. think, be made towards the mitigation of the evils of slavery, and, in time the ultimate abolition of the system, without injustice to any parties interested. The subject is undoubtedly a national question, and therefore it is within the province of the Federal Legislature to entertain it ; and it is the bounden duty of all > the States, whether free or otherwise, to bear their just portion of the evil and its consequences. Let an act (or acts) of Congress then be passed to provide for the following measures on the subject of slaves and slavery : þÿ 1 To prohibit the separation of husband and wife ; and also of children under 14 years of age from their parents. 2 To prohibit torture of any kind to the bodies

of slaves, such as branding, cutting off the cars, <j-c. 3. To limit and restrict the use of the whip, as to the offences for which it may be used, and the number of lashes to be applied. 4 To prohibit dealing in slaves as a trade. 5. To provide for the compulsory release of slaves when demanded, by purchase, on certain conditions to be fixed by act of Congress. The value to be fixed by assessors appointed by the act for each district, who shall determine, from evidence, the price or value to be paid to the owner as consideration for release of the slave. t> To provide that all children of slaves, born after a certain future day, shall be free ; and to provide for their support during infancy. I cannot conceive that any reasonable objection can be offered to any of the above propositions ; and therefore I think, that instead of declaiming against slavery and its abominations, it would bo better to point out a remedy for its evils, and the way of getting rid of it satisfactorily to all part ies, in which the slave-owner will unite with the abolitionist. In that way only can the desired end be attained, without a complete revolution and rupture, if not a civil war in the States. þÿ Yours, respectfully, Philanthropos. Liverpool, Feb 23, 1853.

My declining health again obliges me to leave St. Croix, and with þÿGovernment s permission, in accordance also with the advice of my physician, I now commence a voyage to a northern climate, where once before my failing strength lias been restored. Not being able to take leave of my congregations in their presence, 1 am induced to send them my farewell in writing. First I must not omit with sincere thanks to acknowledge the confidence and favour, which during my stay here His Ex. the Governor has constantly deigned to show me. But gratefully I shall also

always remember the attachment, the kind feel ings and filial devotion, of which on the part of the congregations I so often have gladly received proofs. Many remembrances dear to mo throng before my mind in this hour of parting. The best reward, which at the hands of his flock, a minister can receive, is perhaps a devout attention when he delivers his sermon ; for on this lie will found his hopes, that through his humble means repentance may by the þÿLord mercy s he roused among his listeners, and faith accomplish their salvation. I have not been excluded from such remunerating hopes. In many a house and many a cottage 1 have rejoiced to find faith alive, and been confirmed in that strengthening confidence, that my labours were not in vain. Would that my hopes for the progress of my congregations in faith and true Christian principles may ho crowned with the blessings of Heaven. This is my farewell-wish to You all, who count yourselves members of my fioek, and may God bless the dear island you inhabit ! My office is now surrendered in stronger and abler hands than mine. May the congregations continue to show due attachment to their church and minister, and richly grant to my friend anil successor that host of rewards, of which 1 made mention above.

They have indeed already been referred to in some books of this kind, but often with considerable errors. The present Paper is communicated by Charles C.
