The Dane Gardar, of Swedish origin, was the first Northman who discovered Iceland, in 8tl3. Only a few out-places of this country hail been visited previously, about 70 years before, by Irish hermits. Eleven years subsequently, or in s-7 1 , the Norwegian Ingolf began the colonisation of the country, which was completed during a space of tiO years. The colonists, many of whom belonged to the most illustrious and most civilised families in the North, established in Iceland a flourishing Republic. Here, on this distant islerock, the Old-Northern language was preserved unchanged tor centuries, and here in the Hildas were treasured those Folk-sougs and Folk-myths, and in the Sagas those historical Tales and Legends, which the first settlers had brought with them from their Scandinavian mother-lands. Iceland was therefore the cradle of an historical literature of immense value. The situation of the island and the relationship of the colony to foreign countries in its earlier period, compelled its inhabitants to exercise and developc their hereditary maritime skill and thirst for new discoveries across the great Ocean. As early as the year 877 Gunnbioru saw for the first time the mountainous coast of Greenland. Hut, this land was first visited by Erik the Red, in 983, who three years afterwards, in 98ti, by means of Icelandic emigrants, established the first colony on its south-western shore, where afterwards, in 1121, a þÿBishop See s was founded, which subsisted for upwards of 300 years. The head firths

or bays were named after the chiefs of the expedition, Erik the lied settled in Eriks-firth, Eiuar, Kafn and Ketil in the firths called after them, and lleriulf on lleriulfsnes. On a voyage from Iceland to Greenland this same year (980), Biarne, the son of the latter, was driven far out to sea towards the south-west, and for the first time beheld the coasts of the American lands, afterwards visited and named by his countrymen. In order to examine these countries more narrowly, Leif the Fortunate, son of Erik the Red, undertook a voyage of discovery thither in the year 1000. lie landed on the shores described by Biarne, detailed the character of th .se lands more exactly and gave them names according to their appearance : Ilclluland ( New f cm ndla ad) was so called from its flat stones, Markland ( New Scotland) from its woods, and Vineland (New England) from its vines. Here he remained fur some time and constructed large houses, called after him Lcifsbyudir (Leifs Booths). A German, named Tyrker, who accompanied Leif on this voyage, was the man who found the wild vines, which ho recognised from having seen them in his own land, and Leif gave the country its name from this circumstance. Two years afterwards þÿLeif s brother, Thorwald, repaired thither, and in 1003 caused an expedition to be undertaken to the south, along the shore, but lie was killed in the summer of 1004 on a voyage northward, in a skirmish with the natives. The most distinguised however of all the first

American discoverers is Thorfin Knrlsefnc, an Icelander, whose genealogy is carried back in the Old-Northern annals to Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Scottish and Trisli ancestors, some of them of royal blood. In 1000 this chief on a merchant-

voyage visited Greenland and there married Gudrid, the widow of Thorstein (son of Erik the Red) , who had died the year before in an unsuccessful expedition to Vineland. Accompanied by his wife, who encouraged him to this voyage, and by a crew of 1 GO men on board three vessels, he repaired in the spring of 1007 to Vineland, where he remained for three years, and had many communications with the aborigines. Here his wife Gudrid bore him a son Snorrc, who became the founder of an illustrious family in Iceland, which gave that island several of its first Bishops Ilis þÿdaughter son s was the celebrated Bishop Thorlak Runolfson, who published the first Christian Code of Iceland. In 1 121 Bishop Erik sailed to Vineland from Greenland, doubtless for the purpose of strengthening his countrymen in their Christian faith. The notioes given by the old Icelandic voyagechroniclers respecting the climate, the soil and the productions of this new country are very characteristic. Nay, we have even a statement of this kind as old as the eleventh century from a writer not a Northman, Adam of Bremen; lie states, on the authority of Svend Estridson the king of Denmark, a nephew ofCanute the Great, that the country got its name from the vine growing wild there It is a remarkable coincidence in this respect that its English rc-discoverers, for the same reason, name the large island which is close off the coast Martha's Vineyard. Spontaneously growing wheat (maize or Indian corn) was also found in this country.

In the mean time it is the total result of the nautical, geographical and astronomical evidences in the original documents, which place the situation ofthe countries discovered beyond all doubt The number of þÿdays sail between the several newly-found lands, the striking description of the coasts, especially the white sand-banks of New Scotland and the long beaches and downs of a peculiar appearance on Gape God (the Kialarncs and Furdustrandir of the Northmen) are not to be mistaken. In addition hereto we have the astronomical remark that the shortest day was 9 hours long, which fixed the latitude of þÿ41 24 þÿ10 or , just that of the promontories which limit the entrances to Mount Hope Bay, where þÿLeif booths s were built, and in the district around which the old Northmen had their head establishment, which they called Iliip.

At Antigua, the public business was interrupted by the arrival of the new Treasurer, Mr. Price, appointed by the Golonial Secretary, whom the House of Assembly are unw illing to receive or recognise On the offer of two gentlemen as his sureties, according to the requirements of the law, they were rejected, and a memorial got up, to be forwarded to the Queen, against the appointment, which, it appears, the Colonial Secretary acknowledged he hail made in ignorance of the circumstances, and misled by the information ho had received respecting the gentleman, Mr. Sherrington, appointed by the Governor, to succeed provisionally to the place, on the death ofthe former holder (Mr. Musgrave), who had filled a subordinate situation in the same office for 35 years, with credit to himself, and to the general satisfaction ofthe public: a claim which was now put aside in favor of another person, altogether unknown in Antigua. This has naturally given rise to great dissatisfaction and excitement. For our part,, we think it right that, the Colonial Secretary should be made aware of the strong feeling that, exists, not only in Antigua, but we believe in all the colonics, against the appointments to situations in them of trust, and emolument, being given away in England to his friends and retainers, or to the clerks in his office, and their friends and connexions, to the prejudice of the most deserving persons on the spot, who have for years done the most laborious part of the duties of these offices,

and arc perfectly acquainted with the details, as well as fully competent to discharge all the duties ofthe office. This is a custom most, injurious in its effects upon young men of tab at in the colonics , who arc forced to look for employment in othci ways, and not in the public offers, from the best situations in which they must expect to be excluded , howercr deserring of them they may prove Ihemselrcs. It is injurious to them, and unjust to the colonies ; and we trust that an appeal to the Ministry will not prove unavailing ; but that a rule will be established, not of course to prevail without exception, but a general rule, that where a situation becomes vacant in the colonies, it shall be given to the person considered most deserving of it by the Governor, upon whom will be the responsibility of making the appointment. þÿ Barbados IVcst Indian

Her þÿLadyship health s had been for some time past very indifferent, and an attack of Thrush, although successfully combatted by medical skill, had reduced her to so weak a state, that a change of air seemed the only chance of recovery. From the Lnm /on Times, March 1(5, 1853. AUSTRALIA. (from our own correspondent.) MELBOURNE, Jan. 1. Much dissatisfaction and disappointment have been felt and expressed here at the irregularity of the steamers from England, some of them having been beaten by sailing vessels, and it appears that better arrangements must be made by the companies in England us to securing a full supply of coals at the different stations before any dependence can be placed on the passage being made within the time anticipated of 60 to <55 days. I have no doubt that this, as well as the other minor causes which have, as yet, interfered with the steamers accomplishing a quick voyage, will he soon removed, as experience points out what requires to be done. In regard to the general aspect of affairs, there is nothing to report materially different from the accounts I have before given you. The same astonishing I

3 a. þÿ m © tt ¬ X ATIt 3. amount of immigration continues ; the same commercial activity prevails. The high rates of provisions and house-rents are nearly as then, with a decline among a few articles of the former, such as the important one of Hour, which is now selling at about 20/. a-ton, with Is. 6d. the quartern loaf, instead of 40/. the ton, and 2s. 6d. the quartern loaf, as recently charged. Another article of nearly the same daily use þÿ namely, butter, maintains the same price (3s. per lb.); and, as to vegetables and fruit, the prices are quite prohibitory, except to those whose large incomes make the price of living no object. The proceeds from the goldfields seem of late to be somewhat less in quantity; but to this l attach no importance whatever, as it is, in my opinion, one of those slight variations in the amount of supply which in all similar great works of labour must temporarily occur. My belief is that the goldfields of Australia are of such an extent that they will yield the precious metal in at least the same proportion as hitherto for centuries to come. But this is a very different question from the certainties of individual success, and upon this branch of the subject it would he well for thousands if the actual facts of the case were more clearly understood, for in that event a great loss of time, health, and money, would unquestionably be saved. It cannot be too often impressed on the minds of all who meditate emigration to this country with a view to the gold diggings, that it is neither more

nor Jess than a perfect lottery. Although of course, the chances are in favour of those possessing much phvsical strength to enable them to cope with the severe bodily labour which they must necessarily undergo, yet, even with these, it is still the same kind of gambling speculation. A party of four may work for six weeks and get nothing, and, after leaving in disappointment and disgust, the last hole dug by them may be occupied by new comers, who in 24 hours may turn up several pounds weight of gold. The only way to insure a fair digging as a regular trade to go to the degree of success is to þÿ conduct gold diggings with means sufficient to hold on in case of disappointment, and to continue steadily at it in spite of failure, whether it be for three, six, nine, or even 12 months. The result will he then, that you will almost certainly be rewarded with a certain portion of the yellow metal, equivalent to what in England would undoubtedly be rightly considered a large sum, but which, recollecting the high prices the digger has to pay for his provisions, Ac., is, after all, not so large a sum as at lirst sight appears. From conversations with many who have tried their fortunes in the gold regions of Mount Alexander, Bendigo, Forest Creek, Ac., I cannot but come to the conclusion that, speaking generally, the present average wages of labour m Melbourne will prove equally remunerative, without the privations anil severe work which the pursuit of the gold digger involves.

Since my former letter the contemplated export duty on gold has been abandoned, and I am glad it has been so, for the opposition to it on the part of the diggers would in all probability have brought on a collision with the authorities. A meeting was held, at which opinions were expressed that no more license-money should be paid on the Export Duty Bill becoming law; and although, in the event of a disturbance, there could be no doubt of the eventual triumph of law and order, yet it is fearful to contemplate what scenes of bloodshed might have taken place, if so small a force of military and police as exists

here were brought into contact with the large army of diggers which is encamped on those localities which I have mentioned. All public works remain at a standstill ; nothing is doing to meet the pressing demand for the cleansing and sewerage of the city, or for the better supply of water to the inhabitants, who who arc still compelled to resort to the expensive and inconvenient mode of having it brought in watcrcarts, after which it requires filtering, unless you prefer taking the chance of dysentery and other diseases. Whatever faults, however, the Government may be justly chargeable with, 1 am of opinion that they are entitled to much credit for having preserved the tranquillity and peace of this most important colony in the midst of circumstances of danger and difficulty ; anil let those who might, at the first glance, be disposed superficially to underrate such difficulty and danger, rellect on the present disproportion between the amount of physical force at the disposal of the Government and the independent armed masses who are excavating the mineral riches of the colony. It is quite certain that persons, in considerable numbers, are weekly arriving who are quite unsuited to the place, and who must either return or go into occupations they will find very uncongenial. For clerks and dcskmcn there is really no room whatever ; and, it such will, in spite of warning, still come out, they must either endure the hardships, and take the chances of the diggings, or spread them-

selves over the country as farm servants and other labourers. There is nothing else for them, unless indeed menial labour in Melbourne itself, for which, certainly, at present, high wages are freely given. If a man leaving England, where lie has been filling a respectable situation as clerk or bookkeeper, has no objection to come out here and become a þÿ hewer of wood and drawer of þÿwater, by all means let him come ; and lie is pretty sure to do well, for all kinds of mechanical and common labour arc paid for highly; but, let him thoroughly understand this, and not delude himself with the idea that his knowledge of accounts and good penmanship will get him any remuneration equivalent to the great expense of living here. There is a certain limited demand for this latter kind of employment, and good salaries arc obtained for a small number in the banks and þÿmerchants offices as well as in Government situations; but they form so small a proportion of the great numbers who are out here, seeking in vain for similar occupation, that I would strongly advise no further emigration of that class. The bay is crowded with shipping, and contains at this time, as 1 was assured by a captain of one of them, some of the finest ships to be found in any harbour in the world. The number of emigrants and the quantity of merchandise weekly poured into this place from the vessels which arrive daily are truly wonderful. As yet, there seems no excess of the one over the other. Goods

fetch remunerating prices, and the vast multitude, in some way or other, find the means of living; but it is evident that the hinge upon which the stability of the whole turns is the continuance of the gold wealth. If that were to fail, indescribable would he the consequent panic and ruin ; but, as I have before said, believing that there is not the slightest ground for supposing that the gold regions (working and to be worked) will cease to yield their average returns for a very long period, I look on the commercial and general prosperity of the colony as standing on a secure foundation.

Another Break-down ok the Steamer Australian. þÿ The Australian, royal mail steamer, Captain lloseason, returned to Plymouth Sound on Monday morning, at eight þÿo clock.It appears that the vessel had gone about 250 miles lie fore it was necessary to return, under circumstances which will be best understood by the following statement, taken from the lips of one of the passengers, in the presence of the other passengers : þÿ We left Plymouth on Thursday last, at five þÿo clock in the afternoon, and went on all well until the following (Friday) afternoon, when it was found the feedpipes would not supply water to the boilers. The engines were consequently stopped. We were at this time about 250 miles from Plymouth, on the skirts of the Bay of Biscay. It came on a calm, and we could make no progress, for 10 or 12 hours. Attempts were made to start the engines, hut the supply of water from the feed-pipes being insufficient, steam could not be kept up. In the meantime it was found that there were about three feet of water in the engineroom, and the passengers were compelled to join the crew in working the pumps. When the steam was not up there was only one pump besides the fire-engine that could be worked for the engine-room compartment of the vessel. Even when the donkey-engine and the fire-engine worked together the water gained upon us. Some of the secondclass passengers were pumping 24 consecutive hours þÿ the whole of one night and part of another. Eventually the

engines were made to work by leading the feed-pipes to one boiler. By tins means, after putting about, we were enabled to return at half speed, until a breeze sprung up, which enabled us to make greater way. The saloons and all the cabins were running with water, and the water-closets were in a very bad þÿcondition. It will he seen by the proceedings in the House of Commons, on Tuesday evening, that the government intend to put in force the penalties to which the company were liable under their contract. þÿ tV. fy S. From the London Times , March 16, 1853 AUSTRALIA. (prom our own correspondent.) ADELAIDE, Dec. It;. The chief topics of interest here for some time past have been much the same as those which have occupied general attention in England þÿ viz., gold and politics. From all appearances, it would seem that the former of these topics has absorbed a much larger share of conversation in private and comment in public, and given rise to much more extensive action with you than with us Here the treasures of the earth arc now regarded very coolly ; and a growing disposition is manifesting itself to return with greater assiduity than ever to ordinary industrial pursuits. The South Australian diggings at Echunga have proved, so far, to be just what I stated in a former letter þÿ rich enough to keep quiet people in the neighbourhood of their homes, hut not rich enough to attract, hither hordes of vagabonds from all corners of the world. The armed escorts still travel regularly from Bcndigo and Mount Alexander to Adelaide, bringing bcre to wives and families the products of the labour of their absent heads. The Assayoffice has nearly done its work, and will probably die out at the time which was originally named as the limit of its existence þÿ the 28th of January next. Gold tokens of 1/. value (estimating standard gold at 71s. per ounce) arc now issued from the Assay-office, but do not find their way into circulation, inasmuch as coin of the realm is now sufficiently plentiful to meet the ordinary demands of business. Our merchants and capi-

talists have begun to discover that it is wiser policy to send their gold to Britain, in exchange for specie, than to convert it into South Australian sovereigns. The cry for a Mint is consequently very much on the decline, the business of the Assay-office materially reduced, and the shipments takes Sydney of golddust largely increased. The from Adelaide 97,000 ounce s of gold, a quantity larger than lior freight from Sydney and Melbourne combined. In political matters there is absolutely nothing stirring. The Legislative Council was prorogued on the 2d inst., until May next, and with the dispension of that, body ceased. excitement altogether our political Indeed, during activity and the last session of the Council its proceedings attracted very little attention from the public, and even the exciting topics of political reform and self-government, while under discussion in the house, failed entirely to rouse party feeling out of doors. One public meeting, attended by about 70 persons, and two petitions, neither of thcni having more «tlian 200 signatures, were all tin tokens of animation elicited from the people. The enemies of popular rights wish it to he understood that this apathy indicates unfitness for selfgovernment, but the fact is it springs entirely from preoccupation. Our commercial and social perturbations are not yet, sufficiently soothed to allow of devotion to subjects of less immediate and more public interest. The influenza has been frightfully prevalent

here, as well as in all the settlements The tinent, within the last three months. on this con- epidemic docs not seem to have been so fatal here as in the sister colonies, having carried off very few adults in South Australia. Many children, how-

ever, have died. I am glad to say that the malady is now considerably on the decline. A good notion of the commercial condition of the colony may be gained from the Customs' returns for the last quarter, which I have condensed from the Government Gazette. The total value of the quarter's imports was 239,213/. 4s. 8d. This sum includes an item of 86,618/. lis. under the head of coin and bullion. The duty payable on this amount was 26,298/. Os. 7d. The total value of the exports amounted to 306,021/. 14s., including 171,848/. 16s. in bullion and coin. The imports re-exported were valued at 17,744/. 18s. Deducting this item, and the amounts of coin and bullion, it will be found that the imports consumed and remaining in the colony amount to 134,650/. Os. 8d., and the exports, the produce of the colony, to 116,428/. The returns contain also a tabular statement of immigration and emigrants, from which it appears that our population has been increased by the addition of 1 ,525 souls dnring the quarter, the number of arrivals being 5,S07, and the number of departures 4,282. January 8. I have but little to add to my letter of the 16th ult., which I have detained for the Chusan. She is now here, and will leave 1'ort Adelaide this evening. Another illustration of the justice of our complaints respecting steam communication is afforded by the Melbourne. She has not yet arrived, and when she does come she will, I presume, bring us news only to the 3d of October, whereas we are already in receipt of news from

England to the 5th of October, brought by a sailing vessel, the St. George, to Melbourne, and thence here. Sailing vessels, on a circuitous route, seem to beat steamers on a direct one. There is a great demand for labour here, and wages arc very high. Mechanics are receiving from 16s. to 20s. per day, and unskilled labourers from 10s. to 15s. Domestic servants command 9s. per week readily, and even the rubbish and refuse that wo get under the name of needlewomen arc eagerly sought after. It is, however, only to supply a temporary emergency, and great permanent mischief is being entailed upon this colony by dirceting upon it a stream from the sowers of your largo towns and workhouses. Depend upon it, it is a popular error, and a serious one too, that the people who are inherently useless at home can be made valuable here. Hurra shares have experienced a slight decline. They have been up to 158/. ; they stand now at 150/. Golddust sells readily at 72s. Flour is selling at 19/. to 20/. per ton. The rate of interest varies from 8 to 20 per cent., according to the security offered and amount required. -««<«
From Bell's Weekly Messenger, January 15. A True Story of Slave Life. By William Wells Brown.

In October of 1 844, amongst a number of slaves who were exposed for sale at a slave auction in Richmond, Virginia, was a woman of middle size, slin, and delicately built Her skin was lighter than many a northern brunette's, and licrfeaturcs were oval, with thin lips ; indeed many thought no African blood coursed through her veins. The day was as fine as one could wish to behold. The auctioneer's flag hung listless by the pole, and not a breeze had leave to stir. The white slave girl, with tears in her eyes, hammer in hand, began with, " Who bids for this ascended the auction block, and the auctioneer, nice young woman ? How much gentlemen Ileal albino, fit for a fancy girl for any one. She enjoys good health, and is an excellent house servant. How much do you say " Five hundred dollars. ' u < )nly five hundred for such a girl as this ? Gentlemen, she is worth double that sum. 1 am sure if you knew the superior qualities of the girl yon would give more. Here, gentlemen, I hold moral þÿcharacter in my hand a paper " certifying "Seven hundred." "Ah, that she has a good gentlemen, that is something like. This paper hundred." " She is a devoted also states that she is very intelligent." " Eight Christian, and perfifty," exclaimed a second. " Ten fectly trustworthy." "Nine hundred." "Ninesaid a third, and the woman was struck hundred," off to the last bidder for one thousand dollars. This was a southern auction, at which the bones, muscles, sinews, blood, and nerves of a young lady of
twenty-eight years of age sold for fivT hundred dollars ; her moral character for two hundred dollars ; her improved intellect for another hundred ; and her þÿChristianity the person of Christ in his

& <b m <D a: A T LC 3 follower þÿ for two hundred more. The woman had scarcely descended from the auction-block, when a little girl, ten years of age, took her place, and the auctioneer announced her for sale. The child was perfectly white, and all seemed surprised at the announcement that she was a slave. Among the crowd of spectators was a gentlemanly-looking man, apparently about fifty years of age, remarkable for his snow white hair and red face. Upon this man the eyes of the slave woman were fixed, and even the child watched him so attentively that it was remarked by many, lie was the owner of the mother and the father of the child. The good qualities of the little girl were vividly pourtrayed by the auctioneer, but as no one bid for her, the sale closed, and she followed her master home again. The mother, who had been sold to a negro speculator, was placed in prison until his gang was ready to depart for the cotton, sugar, and rice districts. The next day was the Sabbath, and the bells called to mass and prayer meeting. Methodists sang, Baptists immersed, and Presbyterians sprinkled, while the poor slave mother lay on the scanty straw of her dungeon, uncared for even by those who professed the same faith and belonged to the same church as herself. This woman had been housekeeper to her owner, and he had formed a matrimonial alliance with a lady in the neighbourhood, one of the conditions of which was that the housekeeper and her child should be sent oft' before the arrival of the bride. The child

not being sold, her unfeeling father resolved to send her off- with a family who were on the eve of a journey to the northern states; and a few days after, the little slave girl was left in Lombardstreet, Philadelphia, a district in which the coloured people reside. No provision was made for her maintenance, and she was left without a change of clothing. In this forlorn condition she was met by Robert Purvis, Esq., a philanthropist distinguished for his goodness of heart, and certainly tbi> most accomplished coloured gentleman in the United States. Mr. Purvis took the little girl into his own family, where she remained about four years, receiving the same attention and education as his own children, and in 18 18 he placed her in the family of his father-in-law, the late venerable James Fortcn. Mrs Fortcn became much attached to her, and learning the address of her father; she resolved to write to him, and to attempt to awaken in his breast a feeling for his child ; she accordingly wrote, but received no reply. However, she continued to write, until at last answer came that Mr. Carter would pass through Philadelphia in the course of a few weeks, on his way to the springs of Saratoga, and would call upon her. It was on a fine day in the latter part of July, when the street bell summoned the servant to the door, and a gentleman presented himself, who inquired for Mrs. Forten His tall stature, white hair, and ruddy complexion announced him at once as Mr Carter. Being shown into the draw-

ing room, lie was received by Mrs. Forten, who said, "I presume, daughter ?" " I have sir, you are anxious to see your no daughter here," replied the slaveholder; " but having learned from your letters that there is a girl here who was raised on my farm, 1 have called to see her." He seated himself on the sofa, and awaited the entrance of the girl, lie had pictured in his mind's eye the little slave girl of 10 years old, with short hair, dressed in the homespun attire in which lie last saw her on his tobacco plantation in Virginia. A lew moments elapsed when the door opened and Miss Carter entered. She was tall, with prominent features, dark hair, hazel eyes, Grecian nose, mouth rather large, line set of teeth, as white as snow, a turned and well-rounded chin þÿ -in short, her whole countenance had an appearance of beauty seldom seen in any except the quadroon girls of America. Yet she was so white that no one would suppose for a moment that a drop of negro blood flowed through her veins. As she had resided for or six six years in the refined and educated families is of the Fortcn's Foi and Purvis's, she had lost the uncouthncss of the Southern slavegirl, and her manners were easy, graceful, and pleasing. Such was the appearance of Elizabeth Carter when she entered the room, to behold for the first time, after a lapse of six years, the man who, though her own father, had thrown her upon the bosom of a cold and unfeeling world. Her appearance contrasted so strangely with what she

was when he last saw her, that Mr. Carter, though remaining seated on the sofa, with an apparent determination not to stir from his seat, or even give his daughter a nod of recognition on her entrance, arose, bowed, and seemed bewildered at the appearance of the young lady. Miss Carter " seated The protection you denied me I have found herself near Mrs. Forten, as if to say, among strangers " Silence followed the entrance

of the young lady, so that for some moments not a word was spoken ; at last Mrs. Forten turned, and was in the act of speaking to Mr. Carter, when she saw that lie was weeping. The sweet smile, the innocent look, and girlish beauty of the discarded child had touched the finer feelings of the father ; the hard heart melted to tears, and the man took the place of the slaveholder. Mrs. For- ten rose from her seat, and said, " L will leave you with your daughter." Miss Carter was asked by her father to take a seat on the sofa beside him, and an hour after Mrs. Forten was called in, and the father said to his child, " Lizzy hereafter you may call nie father." The expense of the girl's maintenance up to that time was paid, and her future support and education were amply provided for. During the summer of 1S18, while on a visit to Philadelphia, I met with and was introduced to Miss Carter; and when informed that she had been a slave I could scarcely believe that a lady endowed with such rare accomplishments had ever been a victim to inhuman institution from which I had myself escaped only a few years before.

Celestial Tactics. þÿ Among the Chinese, in our city, many amusing scenes occur in their attempts to adapt themselves to our manners and customs and way of doing things. There is no better fun than to see a Celestial on horseback, especially if the animal is any way vicious or refractory. Upon two or three occasions we have noticed them in that particular fix, though it was impossible not to sympathise with them in their terrible and unpleasant situation. Now and then one, in taking a morning ride or turning out upon a public occasion, mounts a spirited animal, and never for a moment thinks of navigating by the reins. They take a death grip with both hands on the pummel of the saddle, and sit and shout aloud in an unknown tongue, while the animal uses his own pleasure as to his speed or direction to travel. A few evenings since a large crowd had collected on Montgomery-street to witness the tactics of some Celestials, who were endeavouriujt O to manage a horse attached to a loaded dray. The horse was gentle and submissive, ami would move right along, but every now and then some one of the party would sing out some awful word, which would cause the animal to back until the dray touched the side walk. Thus was repeated for an hour, till at length one of the bystanders took pity on the Celestials, and drove the animal according to established Jcliu principles. þÿ .SV/ Francisco Paper.

He performed his duty with great promptness, and his language and demeanour generally wore such as to command our admiration. Having paid him for his trouble, the following conversation took place : þÿ ' How long have you been in this city ?' we inquired. ' Twelve months to-morrow, sir,' he politely replied. sugar cam:. The history of sugar cane is involved in great obscurity. It appears to have been imperfectly known to the Greeks and Romans, as Theophrait as a sort of " honey extracted from canes, or dus, who lived 320 years before Christ describes reeds." And Strabo, who states, on the authority of Nearchus, the commander of the fleet in " reeds in India yield honey without bees." We the expedition of Alexander the Great, says that are also informed, that sugar or sugar candy, has been made in China from very remote antiquity ; and that large quantities of it have been exported from India, in all ages, whence it is most probable that it found its way 'to Rome. Sugar cane occurs in a wild state on many of the islands in the Pacific, but in no part of the American continent, notwithstanding a contrary opinion has been expressed. Its cultivation, and the manufacture of sugar, were introduced into Europe from the East, by the Saracens, soon alter their conquests, in the ninth century. It is stated by the Venetian historians, that their countrymen imported sugar from Sicily, in the twelfth century, at a cheaper rate than they could obtain it from Egypt, where it was then extensively made. The first plantations in Spain were at Valencia ; but they were extended to Granada, Mcrcia, Portugal, Madeira, and the Canary Islands, as early as the beginning of the fifteenth century. From Gomera one of these islands, the sugar cane was introduced into the West Indies, by Columbus, in his second voyage

to America in 1493. It was cultivated to some extent in St llomingo, in 1506, where it succeeded better than in any of the other islands. In 1518, there were twenty-eight plantations in that colony, established by the Spaniards, where an abundance of sugar was made which, for a long period, formed the principal part of the European supplies, llarbadoes, the oldest English settlement in the West Indies, began to export sugar in 1646, and in the year 1676, the trade required four hundred vessels averaging one hundred and fifty tons burden. The introduction of sugar cane into Florida, Texas, California and Louisiana, probably dates back to their earliest settlement by the Spaniards or French. It was not cultivated in the latter, however, as a staple product before the year 1 75 1 , when it was introduced, with several negroes, by the Jesuits, from St. Domingo. They commenced a small plantation on the banks of the Mississippi, just above the old city ofNcw Orleans. The year following, others cultivated the plant and made some rude attempts at the manufacture of sugar. In 1758, M. Dttbreuil established a sugar estate on a large scale, and erected the first sugar mill in Louisiana, in what is now the lower part of New Orleans. His success was followed by other plantations, and in the year 1765 there was sugar enough manufactured for home consumption ; and in 1770, sugar had become one of the staple products of the colony. Soon after the revolution a large number of enterprising adventurers emi-

grated from the 1 nited S'tates to Lower Louisiana, where, among other objects of industry, they engaged in the cultivation of cane ; and by the year 1803, there were no less than eighty one sugar estates 011 the Delta alone. Since that period, while the production of cane sugar has been annually increasing at the South, "the manufacture of maple sugar has been extending in the North and West. The common sugar cane is a perennial plant, very sensitive to cold, and is, therefore, restricted in its cultivation to regions bordering on the tropics, where there is little or no frost. In the Eastern hemisphere its production is principally confined to situations favorable to its growth, lying between the fortieth parallel of north latitude and a corresponding degree south. On the Atlantic side of the Western continent, it will not thrive beyond the thirty-third degree of north latitude and the thirty-fifth parallel south. On the Pacific side it will perfect its growth some five degrees

3 A T a 3 further north or south. From the flexibility of this plant, it is highly probable that it is gradually becoming more hardy, and will eventually endure an exposure and yield a profitable return much further north, along the borders of the Mississippi and some of its tributaries, than it has hitherto been produced. In most parts of Louisiana the first season it is denominated " plant cane," and canes yield three crops from one planting. The each of the subsequent growths, "ratoons." But sometimes, as 011 the prairies of Attakapas and Opelousas, and the higher northern range of its cultivation, it requires to be replanted every year. Within the tropics, as in the West Indies and elsewhere, the ratoons frequently continue to yield abundantly for twelve, fifteen, and even twenty-four years from the same roots. The cultivation of this plant is principally confined to the West Indies, Venezuela, Brazil, Mauritius, British India, China, Japan, the Suuda, Philippine, and Sandwich Islands, and to the southern districts of the United States. The varieties most cultivated in the latter are the striped blue and yellow ribbon, or Java the red ribbon, violet, from Java, the Creole, crystalline or Malabar, the Otaheite, the purple, the yellow, the purple-banded, and the grey canos. The quantity of sugar produced on an acre varies from five hundred to three thousand pounds, averaging perhaps, from eight hundred to one thousand pounds. Hitherto the amount of sugar and molasses consumed in the United States has exceeded the

quantities produced ; consequently there has been no direct occasion for their exportation. In the year 1815 it was estimated that the sugar made on the banks of the Mississippi, alone, amounted to 10,000,000 lbs. In 1818, the entire crop of Louisiana was only 25,000,000 lbs. ; in 1850 it had reached the enormous quantity of 226,001 ,000 lbs., besides about 12,000,000 gallons of molasses According to the census of 1 840 the amount of cane and maple sugar was 155,100,809 lbs., of which 119,947,720 lbs. were raised in Louisiana. By the census of 1850 the cane sugar made in the United States, was 247,581,000 lbs. besides 12,700,606 gallons of molasses; maple sugar, 34,249,886 lbs., amounting to 28 1 ,830, -886 lbs., showing an increase, in ten years, of 126,730,077 lbs.

Application op a Curious Physiological Discovery. þÿ It has long been known to physiologists that certain colouring matters, if administered to animals along with their food, possessed the property of entering into the system and tinging the bones In this way the bones of swine have been tinged purple by madder, and instances arc on record of other animals being similarly affected. No attempt, however, was made to turn tb is beautiful discovery to account until lately, when M. Roulin speculated 011 what might have been the consequences of administering coloured articles of food to silkworms just before spinning their cocoons. His first experiments were conducted with indigo, which he mixed in certain proportions with the mulberry leaves serving the worms for food. The result of this treatment wits successful þÿ he obtained blue cocoons. Prosecuting still further his experiments, I10 sought a red colouring matter, capable of being eaten by the silkworms without injury resulting. He had some difficulty to find such a colouring matter at first, but eventually alighted on the Uignnnia chica. Zachaeus Elizabeth 1 1 i Wonderful In-line; of a Dog. The following instance of the wonder ful instinct of the dog is deserving of record: þÿ A gentleman inGlengyle, which, as our readers are aware, is at the upper end of Loch Katrine, wishing to send a terrier of theDandie Dinmont breed to a friend in Portobello, took the opportunity of a farmer in his neighbourhood going to Edinburgh a few weeks ago, to send Dandie to his new quarters, lie left Loch Katrine side in the afternoon, and arrived at Callendar after it was dark. Remaining there over night, he took the coach with his four-footed companion before daylight next morning þÿ travelled from Stirling to Granton by the steamer, from Granton to Edinburg per rail, and without coming out of the station, took the first train to Portobello, where he arrived the same evening long after dark. Dandie was delivered up to bis new friends, but as he did not seem at all comfortable, he was never allowed to go out alone, or be a moment out of sight. He remained for a few days going out and in with his mistress, but seemed very unhappy þÿ having, doubtless, many long and lingering thoughts of the bonnie bills and heather braes of Glengyle. One night the window of a room in which he was kept was inadvertently left open, and from which he leaped out. Notwithstanding every anxious search and offers of liberal rewards, Dandie could not be found, and was given up for lost. To the surprise of his mistress, however, a letter arrived in a few days from Glengyle, stating he had made his appearance

one evening in his old place at the fireside. On comparing notes, he had been two days and three nights on the road, but whether lie travelled by sea or land, or what may have been his route, remains a mystery, as Dandie is not disposed to tell, only wagging his tail, and no doubt laughing in his sleeve when the subject is broached ; ofcoutse he is more prized by bis first master ever not likely he will than ever, and it is require to take so long journey a again. Had he travelled by land all the way been return might have to Portobello, his accounted for ; but considering that his feet never touched the ground from Callendar till he reached there, and that he was carried the greater part of the way in the dark and through tunnels, we consider this to be one of the most remarkable instances of canine sagacity we have heard of. þÿ North British Daily Mail.

From the St. Thomas Times, April !>. Association in Great llrifain lo promote a cheap and uniform system of Colonial and InterEiational Postage !

An Association formed in England with the object the above heading imports it may easily be conceived would not be long in bringing to its aid powerful and influential adherents ; and we, therefore, observe in a report of a meeting recently held in Edinburgh by the Association, to which was invited the Committee of the Law Amendment Society, the Earl of Granville, Mr. llume, and other men of equal distinction, addressing the meeting at great length upon this very important þÿtopic, the whole bearing of their speeches being to to shew that would result all nations could a cheap and the vast amount of good uniform postage Is- introduced throughout the world ! In this popular movement, we And that all nations, and all communities, especially commercial communities, arc respectfully invited to co-operate and take part with the Association, in the hope of ultimately realising its plans and suggestions. In evidence of the zeal with which the Association labors in the cause, we find its corresponding Secretaries instructed to communicate the views of the Association to every commercial city of any note, whether in the far east or far west. A letter received here, and placed into our bands, contains the following passages : þÿ " 1 " am appointed a local Secretary to the Interna - " tional Postage Association. It would " help the cause materially, T have 110 doubt, " were you bringing the subject under the notice "of the various public Institutions in your " quarter. The Press has taken up the matter

" here, " services and in I St. hope Thomas you will be able to enlist its and the West Indies " generally. You will find the objects of the As- " sociation abundantly explained in pamphlets I " here transmit you. 1 shall shortly send you " a form of Memorial or Petition on the subject." One of the first objects the Association is desirous of obtaining is that of inducing business communities abroad to memorialize the British House of Commons to take into its serious consideration the advantages of a cheap and uniform interna-

tional postal system. We must, however, here stop to question the importance of a memorial from a Danish Colony to an English Parliament in advancing the desires of the Association ; nor do we know that International Law would allow of it. One thing is nevertheless, certain, that no community would be more largely benefitted by a cheap and uniform postage than our own. The commerce of St. Thomas is large ; and the correspondence of this little place, strange as it may appear, extends all over Europe. As a consequence, some portions of its postage must be excessively high ; but whether we can do anything in ameliorating it, is another question. From appearances, however, the Press of England will not be long in combining upon the question, and we know that it seldom combines on any matter that does not soon after become the law of the land. Connected with cheap postage, we copy from dressed to the Editor by ' An Englishman' the Grenada Chronicle the following letter ad- " Sir, þÿ I left home early in the year, at which time the people in the principal towns and cities were exerting themselves by means of public meetings, the adoption of petitions to the Legislature, Ac., in favor of the plan of Ocean Penny Postage, similar to the Inland system that is now, with such general advantage, carried out in England. If the residents in the West India Islands would be benefitted by the change, and I think there is 110 doubt they would be so in a variety of ways, it behoves them to strengthen the

hands of their friends at home, by adopting petitions in the different Islands, and forwarding them to the Peers and Members of Parliament, who are known to be in favor of cheap postage, for presentation. Without going into further particulars, T beg to give this hint to your readers."

A TALE OF THE SEA. It was a bright moonlight evening, and so warm that our men lay about the deck and in groups with hardly any covering ; I think I never saw so perfectly clear and brilliant a night. Some of the officers were reading, and with ease, by the light of the moon ; and the ocean, as far as the sight could stretch, was a glittering mirror without a single ruffle or wave : we lay like a log on the water, with all sails set, but not a breath of air to move them. The crew were collected in small parties about the forecastle and main-deck, listening to the long yarns of some gray-headed seaman, about the Flying Dutchman of the Black River of Gatand, while now and then some favourite sea-song was bawled forth from the laughing crowd. The officers were walking about the quarter-deck, smoking and conversing, and occasionally extending their walk so far as to listen voyage on the wide, wide to the stories of the forecastle. This was my first ' sea,' and as I was the youngest of the mids, I found particular favour with several of the oldest seamen, with whom, by the by, I liked to associate better than with my brother middies. I always loved to listen to their tales of murder and battles, and would sit for hours on the coils of rope, and hear old Jack years, relate his adventures and ' hair-breadth Transom, our second mate, an old man of sixty escapes.' We had left Port Royal, on the south side of Jamaica, the day before, on our way to the mouth of the Amazon, and were now passing between the small islands of Montscrrat and Guadeloupe :

in the distance you could see the white moonbeams playing on the fort and beach, and glistening on the low roofs and white walls of the little capital of G uadeloupe. I was standing on the capstan with a small night-glass in my hand, looking at the opposite shore, with its long low beach, with here and there a small slave-hut or mound of loose stones piled up as a covering over the grave of some drowned sailor whose body had been washed on shore. I dropped my glass, and was getting down from my station, when Jack Transom stepped up, and asked for a squint. I handed the ment, he hauded it back, saying : ' Ay, ay, there glass to him, and after looking through it a moit stands, with its creaking chains and dry bones rattling in the still rippling over it ' ' What's that ?' said I, eagerly p.ir, as if a ten-knot breeze was catching the glass, and pointing it where ' Old Starboard,' as he was familiarly called, directed me. It was some time before I saw what lie meant. When I did, I was at no loss for his abrupt speech. A little north of the town, on the white beach, stood a tall gibbet with its chains, and even, as old Jack said, its white bones, for I plainly saw them even at that distance glimmering in the rays of the bright moon, and I almost fancied I heard them rattling and shaking against each other, though, as I said before, there was not a breath of air, not enough to move a feather. I shuddered at the sight, for I was young, and easily affected by anything terrible or gloomy.

We all knew that Old Starboard was on one of his long-yarn tacks, and in a short time a group was formed around the old fellow, as anxious as the crowds of coffee-drinkers in the saloons of Constantinople to listen to the wonderful adventures of the Caliph Haroun Alraschid, or Sinbad the Sailor. 'It's now forty years ago, or thereabouts,' began Old Starboard, stuffing a huge quid of the true Virginia into his left cheek, 'since I first laid eyes on that same death-telling gallows. I was then a mere foremast-man, and perhaps rather green, seeing as how that was my first tack this way, and only the third time I had ever smelt salt water. It was a dark stormy night, with a strong north-wester blowing at the rate of ten knots an hour, and we were beating across this very channel uudcr a heavy press, with the hopes of clearing the shoals before morning ; all hands were on deck clearing off and taking in some of our light canvas, for the gale kept on increasing, and our main-mast creaked heavily with its load, when the watch ahead bawled out, " Helm a-lee ! sail ahead !" þÿ hut before the words were scarcely out of his mouth, we were upon the vessel. We struck her about midships, carrying away our bowsprit, and dashing in the forecastle sails and knuckle-timbers as if they had been glass. But it fared worse with the vessel we met. She was small, being about seven feet in the water, whereas we drew nearer fifteen. We passed slick over her, as if she had been a mere boy's plaything.

You maybe sure there was no standing still; everything was hauled up, and we were before the wind in less thau half a shake ; the boats were lowered, although there was such a sea running that it was almost impossible to live in a small boat. Logs of wood and hen-coops were thrown overboard, so that, if any were alive, they might save themselves. Our first mate was standing on

3 tr A T II 3. the quarter, listening, when he declared that he hoard a shout. We listened, and then it came again and again, but fainter every time. At length our captain ordered a boat out, with directions to put in to the shore, and come off in the morning, as we should lay to. That night there was not an eye closed in the ship. We were all waiting for the morning, for many thought it sheer madness in our captain to send off a boat in such a sea, and so dark a night, and prophesied that she would be swamped in less than ten minutes; though no one said so to the captain, for he was in one of his gloomy moods, and walked the deck nearly the whole night without opening his mouth. We stood off and on till morning, and by this time the wind had lulled considerably, and we had a moderate breeze. As soon as it was light, we bore down to the little bay you sec off' yonder to the nor'-cast, and having anchored, sent oft a boat to the shore. I was in her, and I shall never forget my joy when I first saw our men standing on the beach and hallooing to us ; we were soon among them, and asking questions enough to sink a lighter. After leaving the ship, they steered as near as they could tell to where the cries came from ; after running about ten minutes, they could hear them plainer, and at last got so near as to speak to the person : it was a man who was clinging to a large board, and was nearly exhausted. After a time they got him in, and finally reached the shore ; the poor fellow was nearly gone, and could not speak a

word, so they took him to a house, and, after awhile, by rolling and warming him, brought him to. It so happened that the house belonged to the governor, or whatever they call him ; and as soon as he clapped his eyes on the man, he knew him, and had him taken to prison ; and it turned out that, after all our trouble, we had only saved the poor wretch from being drowned that he might be hung ; for it was proved by many who knew him, having seen the fellow before, and by pieces of the wreck which floated ashore, that he was nothing better than a real pirate, whose murders were so numerous they couldn't be counted. He had been taken twice before, but had escaped each time. The governor, to be sure of him, now ordered the execution to take place that day. We had leave to stay on shore and see it. He looked pale and half dead when they brought him out. and for the soul of me 1 couldn't help pitying him, he stepped so firm, and went so willingly to meet his death. He was led out to the gallows between two tiles of soldiers, and our parson talked to him all the way, but he paid no attention, and seemed to be thinking of something else þÿ mayhap the tine vessel he had lost, and all that. We saw the poor fellow swung off', and then went back to our ship, but there was no laughing or joking that day, nor the next either, for we all felt as if we had some hand in it, and wished the poor man had been food for the fishes rather than to have fallen a prey to land-sharks. The body was taken

down, and then hung up in chains ; and on our homeward voyage we saw them there rattling in the Seabreeze and bleaching in the sun I have passed here often, but I have never forgotten and look for the gallows and the pirate's remains, to I shall never forget that night while I live.' ' All hands a-hoy!' shouted the boatswain, and in a moment I was left alone. Before I went to my berth, I took one more look at the dreaded object, and determined, if ever I found leisure, to commit the story to paper. It is precisely because we arc so prone to consider our happiness a thing belonging to the future that we delay the accomplishment of our universal object. Our happiness, social and domestic, lies in truth within our own hearts ; it is with us to-day and as much within our reach as it will ever be, only that the war of strife, the heart burnings, jealousies, doubts, fears, mistrusts, suspicions of humanity unrestrained, stifle the uprising of that spirit of universal charity which is the secret of our delight. As the ricing sun floods a world composed of every shade of beauty ; of wild places, of peaceful haunts, filled with ineffable splendour ; brightens with its invisible touch the most gloomy recesses ; penetrates the black forests where deeds of sin and crime have been perpetrated, so our own soul can brighten the spot, the people, and the things on which it looks. We mistake our desire too frequently, because we do not understand either ourselves or one another. The pride of man restrains some of his noblest impulses, thoughts, wishes, and intentions, within his own breast, simply because too often he thinks others will misunderstand them, and because now is not the proper time to reveal them. He feels that if a grand occasion were to arise for the display of some consummate virtue, he should he found ready with his sacrifices, his self dcuials, his devotion ; but the noblest sacrifices demanded by our social condition arc those which we make to one another in our daily intercourse. If we look

within our own circle, we shall find that there is hourly need for the full play of our widest charineeded every day not now and then, but in smal- ties þÿ forbearance, þÿ generosity, self sacrifice, are ler degrees every hour ; and it is the practice of these home virtues that will ultimately procure for us the greatest happiness the world can give. We are too prone to place it in possession of wordly gifts ; but since these would demand equally the guardianship of all the human virtues, we are safe in a moderate sphere of existence, determined heart and soul to minister to cacli other's good, to repress all malice, envyings, jealousies, and strife, then we could be surrounded by a host of temptations to evil. We once more repeat, that our chief power of happiness lies within our own hearts, and may be best sought for in homes ; so we do acknowledge that the possession of moderate comfort combines to produce the proper spirit within us. þÿ The. Nation.

Madwig, to the presidency of the Danish Folkething, was the unanimous act of the House; the relative strength of parties has, therefore, yet to he revealed. The Government reckons upon a majority of only 4 or 5 in an assembly of 98 deputies, 27 of whom are new to the Legislature. The letters patent concerning the cession, to the crown of Denmark, of the lands possessed by the Duke of Augustenhurg in the Duchies, have been published at Copenhagen. The Duke promises for himself and his family never to re-enter the Duchies, or to acquire real property there; never to undertake aught against the peace of t he realm, or oppose any measures which may be taken for organising the new monarchy, and regulating its order of succession The Duke receives an indemnity ol'ahout 2, 500, (KM) thalers. The opposition in the Danish Chambers sustained a defeat at the opening. The two Chambers decided to make the question of the order of the succession their first business, and accordingly on the 17th the premier declared it to be the policy of' Denmark definitively to abandon the claim to the borders of the F.idcr. The minority represents the principle of the integrity of the monarchy, and of the exclusion of the female line from the throne, as inscribed in the London convention.

EIRE AT WINDSOR CASTUE. On Saturday night, a few hours after the arrival of the Royal Family at Windsor Castle, an alarming fire suddenly broke out in their private apartments, which are situated in the Prince of Wales's Tower. This tower overlooks Eton College and the terrace flowergarden and slopes, which are so familiar to the daily readers of the Court Circular. On its ground floor stood the Gothic dining-room, a very handsomelydecorated apartment, and here her Majesty and the Prince dined alone on Saturday, as is their custom on the day of their arrival at the Castle. They had concluded their repast, and retired to an adjoining apartment, when dense volumes of smoke suddenly apprised the domestics that a fire had originated behind the woodwork of the diningroom. Every exertion was used to extinguish it, but we regret to s ty that the efforts made were not successful until a considerable destruction of property had taken place. We are glad to be enabled to state that her Majesty has not suffered from this alarming occurrence, and that her wonted self-possession under circumstances so trying did not for a moment forsake her. The fire is said to have originated from a furnaceflue, situated at the basement of the Prince of Wales's Tower, for the purpose of heating the air which warms the Gothic Dining-room, and many other apartments in this tower. No estimate has yet, of course, been formed of the loss, which will fall chiefly on the Lord Chamberlain's department. The most

praiseworthy zeal was exhibited by all engaged in extinguishing the flames; and, with two exceptions of slight injuries, no one appears to have been seriously hurt. The preservation of the castle from the imminent danger which threatened it is naturally a source of special thankfulness to the inhabitants of Windsor, but it will be heard with loyal satisfaction throughout the the destruc- try", in every part of which countion of the greatest of our royal residences would have been received as a national calamity. I lis Royal Highness Prince Albert was present until the last, as were also the Hon. Colonel Grey, the Hon. Colonel Biddulph, and the lion. Colonel Phipps. The (iueen and the Royal Family, who had retired to their private apartments at the south-east part of the castle, remained there tire remain at the Castle. whole of the night. Resignation of Rilio|» Ives. The following letter from Bishop Ives, who has lately joined the Catholic church, is addressed to the Convention of the Protestant Episcopal Church, in the Diocese of North Carolina : Rohf., Wednesday, Dec. 22, 1852. Dear Brethren : Some of you, at least, are aware that for years doubts ol the validity of my office as Bishop have at times harrassed my mind and greatly enfeebled my action. At other times, it is true, circumstances have arisen to overrule these doubts, and to bring to my mind temporary relief. But it has been only temporary, for, in spite of resolutions to abandon the reading and the use of Catholic hooks; in spite of earnest prayers and entreaties that God would protect my mind against the distressing influence of Catholic Truth ; and in spite of public and private professions and declarations, which in times of suspended doubt I sincerely made to shield myself from suspicion and win back the confidence of my diocese, which had been well nigh lost þÿ in spite ol all this, and of many other considerations which would rise up before me, as the necessary consequence of suffering my mind to he carried forward in the direction in which my doubts pointed, these doubts would again return with increased and almost overwhelming vigor, goading me at times to the very borders of derangement. Under these doubts, I desired temporary relief from duties that had become so disquieting to me, and determined to accompany Mrs. Ives, whose health

demanded a change of climate, in a short absence abroad. But absence has brought no relief to my mind. Indeed, the doubts that disturbed it have grown into clear and settled convictions ; so clear and settled that, without a violation of conscience and honor, and every obligation of duty to God and His Church, 1 can no longer remain in my position. called 1 am upon, therefore, to do an act of self-sacrifice, in view of which all other self-sacrificing acts of my life are less than nothing; called upon to sever the ties which have been strengthened by long years of love and forbearance, which have hound my heart to many of you, as was David's to that of Jonathan, and make my heart bleed as my hand traces the sentence which separates all pastoral relation between us, and conveys to you the knowledge that I hereby resign into your hands my office as Bishop of North Carolina ; and further, that I am determined to make my submission to the Catholic Church. In addition (my feelings will allow me only to say,) as of any perception this act is earlier than my own, and antedates, by some months, the expiration of the time for which I asked leave of absence, and for which I so promptly received from members of your body an advance of salary, 1 hereby renounce all claim upon the same and acknowledge myself to bound, wish, return on an intimation of your whatever you may have advanced to me beyond this 22d day ol December. With continued affection and esteem, I pray you to allow me still to subscribe
myself, Your faithful friend, etc. (New York Herald.) L. ."ilLLIMAN 1VKS.
